subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition requested a few days ago and again yesterday that I should outline the main items which the government intends to introduce during the present session. I would say that in addition to the items which are already on the order paper the following will be introduced: the bill of rights, a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, a bill to establish a national energy board, a bill to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act, a bill to provide additional grants to the province of Newfoundland, an amendment to the Bretton Woods Agreements Act; bills respecting the superannuation of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and members of the Canadian forces; a bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act, and a bill to bring in certain amendments to the Criminal Code.
In the field of agriculture, amendments will be introduced to assist the provinces in implementing crop insurance, as well as a bill to extend and improve farm credit facilities, and a bill to allow veteran farmers to take greater advantage of modern agricultural practices will be introduced by way of amendment to the Veterans Land Act.
In addition there will be, of course, the budget legislation and the usual measure respecting the financing of the Canadian National Railways. Consideration is also being given to certain other measures of lesser importance. It is probable that some of these may be introduced before the end of this session. However, if any change is made in this regard ample notice will be given to members of the house.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION
speechtext: No, we are not following that order. I am glad the Leader of the Opposition asked that question.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION
speechtext: In that case I merely express the hope that the Prime Minister and the house leader will put these bills on the order paper in ample time to give us on the opposition side time to study them, because they include some very important pieces of legislation.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION
speechtext: This is a very heavy and exhaustive program which the Prime Minister has outlined, and I hope the legislation can be placed on the order paper as quickly as possible, since it seems, clear that the major part of the business of this session has yet to be done. If the session is not to be of very great duration it will certainly be necessary for hon. members to have this legislation before them as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM FOR SESSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in that connection I am sure all of us are very desirous of assuring that the business of the house will be placed on the order paper and then brought before the house at the earliest possible date.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF COMPOSITION OF ECONOMIC CONSULTATIVE COUNCIL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF COMPOSITION OF ECONOMIC CONSULTATIVE COUNCIL
speechtext:
There is another announcement I should like to make, Mr. Speaker. A corresponding statement was made at 4 p.m. Greenwich mean time in London today. It has to do with the composition of the commonwealth economic consultative council. It will be recalled that by decision reached at the commonwealth trade and economic conference in Montreal last September regarding commonwealth consultation on trade and economic matters there was a statement in the conference report which read in part, as follows:
Commonwealth consultation and co-operation in economic matters are of primary importance in achieving our objectives in the economic field. We are agreed that the present machinery for consultation is working well; it is flexible and informal and well fitted to the family character of the commonwealth relationship. We decided that the existing arrangements should be co-ordinated under the name of a commonwealth economic consultative council.
2878	HOUSE OF
Commonwealth Relations
The conference also agreed that, at the highest level, the council would consist of the finance and economic ministers of the commonwealth countries meeting together whenever the circumstances demanded and that-in the words of the report-it would-[DOT]
[DOT]-incorporate various channels and bodies through which economic consultation at present takes place and any further bodies which may be set up from time to time on a temporary or permanent basis. Meetings at high official level will also be held as necessary to prepare for the meetings of ministers.
Since the Montreal conference there has been an exchange of views regarding the particular commonwealth bodies of officials that should be incorporated within the framework of the council. All commonwealth governments have now agreed that the council should be regarded as also incorporating meetings of senior commonwealth economic officials held to prepare for meetings of ministers, the commonwealth liaison committee, the commonwealth economic committee and meetings of commonwealth statisticians to consider the balance of payments of the sterling area. The inclusion of other commonwealth bodies through which economic consultation takes place will be considered from time to time as seems desirable.
I should emphasize in conclusion that what is being done is to incorporate existing bodies within a new framework rather than to create new bodies. To quote once again from the report of the Montreal conference:
Arrangements which are already extensive have served us well: there is no need to expand them, nor would we wish to change in any way their consultative character.
A meeting of senior economic officials representing commonwealth governments will be held in London starting on May 5, to exchange views on general trade and economic subjects. It is expected to last three or four days. While the composition of the Canadian delegation is not complete, I should advise the house that it will be led by the deputy minister of finance, Mr. K. W. Taylor.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF COMPOSITION OF ECONOMIC CONSULTATIVE COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the house knows, for a great many years now commonwealth ministers in charge of financial and economic matters have been meeting periodically, as have other commonwealth officials in these fields. Various commonwealth economic and other committees were established years ago and have been functioning for many years.
I think of the imperial economic committee, which has been more lately called the commonwealth economic committee, the imperial shipping committees, and others. I gather


from the Prime Minister that no new machinery is being created, but that an effort is being made to co-ordinate and consolidate existing committees.
In so far as this proposal will serve to accomplish that purpose I think it is to be welcomed, but I do not think we should attach too great importance to the fact that this decision has been taken and has been implemented, because commonwealth economic consultation and co-ordination is going on effectively now and has been for a good many years.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF COMPOSITION OF ECONOMIC CONSULTATIVE COUNCIL
speechtext: Any move to streamline any consultation is probably a good thing and certainly welcome as far as we are concerned. I would think that cooperation and consultation amongst commonwealth countries are much more essential now than they have been in the past. Particularly in the field of trade, the commonwealth, Canada included, faces the challenge of the European common market as well as the challenge of the Soviet union. With those great economic challenges facing us at this time, anything that can be done to streamline our methods of consultation and bring about new policies is more than welcome.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 20, consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before I go on with my speech which I started last evening I would like to offer my apologies to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris). I had no opportunity of correcting the proofs of my speech last night, and this morning, to my dismay, I found that Hansard had quoted me as referring to the hon. gentleman as "the shorter member for Halifax". May I assure the hon. member that I certainly had no intention of referring to him in that way. I thought I had referred to him, and I am morally certain I did, as "the hon. member for Halifax".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a point of order. I thank the hon. member for his apology, but that is precisely the definition I would prefer. We have no junior or senior member.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I shall withdraw the apology.
Mr. Speaker, one of the points I was attempting to make last evening was that in its defence of the budget the government is begging the question when it claims that under the circumstances it had no alternative but to have a large deficit. What the Liberal opposition has been saying is that the government has created, and indeed is responsible for, the circumstances in which the government now finds itself. If Canada is burdened with a record deficit and increased taxation it is because the government, in order to save face, has attempted to implement a fraction of the exaggerated promises and commitments which it made during the election campaign, and which the Canadian economy simply could not afford at this time. So I think it is quite clear that the deficit is attributable to the political expediency, to the opportunism, to the lack of wisdom and to the lack of administrative responsibility shown by this government.
When the house rose last evening I was saying that as we look at the deficit, and as we prepare to pay additional taxes, we might well ask ourselves what the government has returned to the people which might explain or justify this huge deficit, and what the government has to show in return for this record peacetime expenditure. Immediately, of course, the members of the government point to the increase in the old age pension, as did the Minister of National Revenue the other evening. In his remarks the minister referred to the increase in the old age pension from $40 to $46 made by the Liberal government as representing two cups of coffee, a slogan which was very widely used during the electoral campaign of 1957. What the minister did not say was that Canada could afford the two cups of coffee at that time, whereas the three cups of coffee which this government has offered in this $9 increase in old age pensions have created a deficit of $184 million in the pension fund which must be paid out of consolidated revenue, and which has necessitated a permanent increase in the special sales tax and income tax earmarked for that purpose.
That is not increasing social legislation, reducing taxes and balancing the budget. Desirable though it may have been to increase old age pensions, this government stands condemned not only for having misled the Canadian people with regard to the economic possibility of an increase in pensions at that time but for having, by its extravagance and ill-timed spending, added to the inflationary tendencies of our economy and detracted from the purchasing power of that very same $9 which was given to help out our senior
The Budget-Mr. Cardin citizens. As a matter of fact the three cups of coffee represented by the $9 increase have now been reduced to only two cups because of the increase in the cost of living.
Can we say that the money involved in the government's deficit has been used in order to stabilize our economy? Where, in fact, is the special billion dollar public works program which the Conservatives claimed would solve the unemployment problem? There is not one indication either in the estimates or in the budget speech that the government has embarked on what is designed to be, or what has turned out to be, a truly visionary program. On the other hand there are indications that unemployment is still rampant in the country and running at an uncomfortably high level for this time of year. We know, of course, that the moneys in the unemployment insurance fund are still below the critical point, yet there is not indication whatsoever of any legislation with regard to unemployment such as was promised in the speech from the throne at the beginning of this session. Can anyone say that our economy is in any way more stable now than it was in 1957?
Similarly, it cannot be claimed that government expenditure has been directed at solving the federal-provincial fiscal problem in such a way that both the provinces and the municipalities would have adequate tax revenues to enable them to meet their constitutional responsibilities. This, again, was promised by the Conservative government.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think it would be very interesting to take a good look at page 2410 of Hansard, where hon. members will find a table headed "federal contributions to the provinces". This is the table to which the Minister of National Revenue referred at page 2628 of Hansard, where he said:
My time is running out but we find that in the 1956-57 fiscal year-just two years ago-the total contribution made two years ago by the treasury of this country, by the minister of finance, by my hon. friend's predecessor, was $689 million. That was the last payment made by the immediate predecessor of my hon. friend. According to the budget which the present Minister of Finance has brought down, for which he is criticized for imposing higher taxes, for which he is criticized because it still has a deficit, which is the situation? According to those figures, for the fiscal year which will end next March 31 the total contributions to the province will be $1,212,500,000, virtually twice the $689 million which was paid three years ago.

The Budget-Mr. Cardin
Evidently in saying this the minister was trying to create the impression that the Conservatives had doubled the federal contributions to the provinces. But he forgot to mention that in arriving at that conclusion he had to include the increases which were made by the Liberal government in the budget of 1957-58 brought down by Mr. Walter Harris. It is not true that the last contribution made to the provinces by the Liberal government was of the order of $689 million, because in the budget of 1957-58 the federal contribution to the provinces was considerably increased.
May I remind hon. members that when the Minister of National Revenue was making this statement he was making it in the House of Commons; he was not making it on a political platform during a political campaign. It would be interesting to hear what Conservative members of the house have to say about the fact that the tax rental agreements and the tax abatements made to the provinces are considered by this government as federal contributions to the provinces, though we, as Liberals, have always acknowledged and recognized that the moneys obtained by the provinces either through the rental of their direct taxing powers or through the abatements applied to the provinces were not a federal contribution but were a direct constitutional right and prerogative of the provinces.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the Conservative members in this house, particularly those from the province of Quebec, who have waxed so eloquent in the past about the necessity for preserving provincial rights and autonomy, do not get up in their places and accuse this government of a most insidious attack on provincial rights, it will be another conclusive proof that provincial rights and provincial autonomy have been used in the province of Quebec as a political warhorse and for political purposes only, and that in spite of the indignant speeches we have heard from these hon. members during election campaigns in the past they have lacked either the courage or the interest to get up and defend their province against a serious and really dangerous infringement of a fundamental constitutional right.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the deficit could be explained on the grounds of a substantial increase in government expenditure in the field of national defence. Here again it should be noted that there is nothing in our national defence policy that warrants the expenditure of $617 million. The government, as we all know, has spent every last cent of the $211,800,000 in the special defence

equipment fund, which if it had not existed would have boosted our national deficit to well over $800 million.
It has been our national defence policy in the past for Canada to participate to the fullest extent it could in maintaining peace either through the medium of the United Nations or through NATO. We have in fact sent Canadian troops to Korea, and we have stationed troops in the Middle East and in Europe in order to prevent aggressive attacks from the U.S.S.R. At a time when it is well known that the dangerous, critical and strategic area is no longer Korea or Europe but indeed is the North American continent; when it is further realized that Canada has virtually become the forefield of United States defence and that in the event of war between the United States and the U.S.S.R. Canada would likely be the battleground of that war and at a time when the security of our very soil is being threatened as never before in the past, this government to all appearances does not seem willing to do as much for the defence of our own land as Canada did in the past for the defence of other lands which were in danger of aggression.
Under this government we have seen a cutback in our militia. Even though experts many times in the past have told us that the best protection against thermonuclear warfare is civil defence, it has not been possible for many months to obtain a report on civil defence so we might know what is or is not being done in this field. We have seen the last CF-100 come oft the assembly lines. We have witnessed the discontinuance of the production in Canada of the Astra control system. We are no longer producing the Canadian Sparrow. We stood by and watched the aerial defence of Canada turned over to the United States. We have discontinued the production of the Canadian Arrow and replaced it with the United States Bomarc because it was cheaper, though everyone knows that by the time our armed forces are equipped with the Bomarc it will be as obsolete as the Arrow would have been.
Just the other evening the hon. member for Quebec South, for whose judgment I have a great deal of respect, stated blandly on a television broadcast that the Sparrow was dropped in order that the government might economize. I have nothing against economizing, but the crippling of our national defence industry and the increasing of unemployment are not my idea of sensible economizing. It would appear that the government has not only placed our national defence policy on a bargain basis, but it does not seem to be willing to pull its own weight in the mutual

defence agreements we have with the United States for the defence of the North American continent. There is no other interpretation to be placed on the fact that the government has nothing to replace either the CF-100 or the CF-105, the discontinuance of which leaves a terrible gap in the strength of our armed forces.
The fact that the government is allowing thousands of scientists, engineers, technicians and skilled labourers to leave our national defence industry is an indication that the government is not planning to continue to any extent the production of Canadian armament for Canadian defence. While we feel that such an attitude is a tremendous blow to the pride we justifiably felt during the war when Canadians were sailing Canadian ships, firing Canadian guns and flying Canadian planes, the government's attitude has struck an even more painful and serious blow to Canadian industry as a whole which was born of the determination and sacrifice of the Canadian people to meet the challenge of that former day with Canadian armaments and equipment, and which indeed resulted in the unprecedented prosperity Canadians have been enjoying until very recent times.
Today it appears that the government has based its national defence policy on a production sharing basis with the United States. Of course the Prime Minister has given us the assurance that Canada will get its fair share of national defence production. I must admit that I am a little sceptical with regard to the Prime Minister's verbal assurances when I recall the assurances he gave to the Canadian people in the autumn of 1957 to the effect that there was no unemployment, and the assurance he gave a little later that while he was Prime Minister not one Canadian would suffer from unemployment.
Several months have passed since the Prime Minister gave the assurance that Canada would receive its fair share of defence production, and as yet there is not one indication that Canada will in fact get its fair share of defence production from the United States. The existence in the United States of the buy American act, the existence in that country of 4,500,000 unemployed, and the fact that a large number of defence industries there are working only part time are causes for anxiety which outweigh the Prime Minister's verbal assurances.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having had the pleasure of sitting through the entire seven days of this debate I believe I may say that the speeches were obviously of two classes. There
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming were those which had something kind to say about the budget, and the other half comprising those which did not have something kind to say about the budget. Throughout I have been literally a captive audience.
Having been on the receiving end for seven days I may be pardoned today if I perhaps seek to reverse the role somewhat. I may comment, however, that I am deeply grateful to hon. members for the many kind things they have said in the course of this debate; I appreciate them very much indeed. If in my remarks today I do not dwell on speeches of that kind, I trust hon. members will realize that the time is limited for dealing with the other half of the speeches.
I may perhaps claim that in the course of the budget debate last year and this year I have learned to become somewhat philosophic and relaxed about that half of the speeches to which I should like now to address myself. A good many of these speeches, of course, have been read. I may be pardoned perhaps for suggesting that I think it would be a good thing if Professor Lamontagne would vary his style a little from speech to speech. A variation of that kind, rather than monotony, is a desirable thing in a ghost writer. There was one outstanding exception, of course, and that was the speech made by my good friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who refreshed us all yesterday with his intervention in this debate, interspersed as it was with copious-or should I say "liberal"-statistics drawn from that unique source, the Martin bureau of statistics.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, after listening to the debate for these past seven days I may say, I hope not immodestly but out of conviction, that if I were bringing in a budget tonight it would be the same budget I had the honour to introduce in this house on the evening of April 9.
The house has before it, sir, an amendment introduced on behalf of the official opposition. It purports to ask the house to express regret that the government has shown bad faith. Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to examine this amendment and to search it from end to end for any statement of principle in regard to those matters that receive attention in it, namely taxes, expenditures, a balanced budget. What is the principle that the official opposition inserts in its amendment? What would it-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That politicians should carry out their promises.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-introduce by way of a budget, Mr. Speaker? What would be the guiding principle or policy of its budget if it were in a position to bring one in? Mr. Speaker, you can read this amendment a thousand times, and you will know just

as much at the end as to what was in the minds of hon. members opposite as when you began. There is no policy. They have not ventured to say where they stand on questions of taxes, or expenditures, or balancing of the budget. Therefore we are entitled to say to them at this time, when they have had the opportunity given to them under the rules of this house to state their policy, to state their position, to give the features of the budget they would have introduced: what would they have done had they been bringing in the budget? Rather the theme on the part of hon. members opposite has been that the people should not have elected the government. From member after member we have heard them deliver reproaches upon the electorate. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is well that we should have an understanding of some features of this democratic system of ours. Hon. members opposite had better learn soon that the people, the sovereign people, are supreme in this country, and it will reflect no credit upon the opposition to exert themselves to deliver reproaches upon the people of this country for their decision.
And so, Mr. Speaker, we have listened on the part of hon. members opposite to a series of what might be called hit and run speeches, because they have run right away from anything approaching a statement of their position on those important issues confronting the Canadian people. They have run away from reality; they have expressed no concern over such matters as inflation and other major problems.
I do not wish to overlook any hon. members opposite. In the course of this debate I think we have seen on the part of the C.C.F. group the same willingness to go blithely along proposing measures regardless of whether they would destroy initiative and enterprise, or whether they would harm the economy. It has been the old picture of pie in the sky, a sky full of pie, and pie that never has to be paid for.
Well, so much for them. As for the official opposition, Mr. Speaker, they have floundered in their own pretences; they have thought apparently they could somehow skate through eight days of debate without ever exposing their own views on those important questions. One of them said I had to walk a tight rope in this debate. Mr. Speaker, I may have had some difficulties to deal with in framing this budget, but believe me the tight rope walking in this debate has been done by hon. members opposite. Indeed, sir, in the way they have threaded their way around and away from those important issues they have, I suppose, earned for themselves the title of "the pick and choose company".

Now, evidently having no policy of their own to offer, I do not blame them for whatever they wish to say about us in the light of what we may have said on other occasions. But, Mr. Speaker, that is a far cry from what has been done by hon. members opposite with statements made in the past by members of the government and others who are sitting to your right. We have watched them in this debate wrench statements out of their context, twist them out of all resemblance, divorce them from the time and circumstances related to them, while they have not said anything about their own past statements. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I may be forgiven if today I seek to remind them of some of the things they have said in times past and undoubtedly would like to forget today.
There is one feature, Mr. Speaker, that stands out above all others in the attitude of the official opposition in this debate. It is this, Mr. Speaker, and it is a sad fact. The Liberal party, as represented by its speeches in this house, is today at odds with the Canadian people. The partisan interests of the Liberal party have been demonstrated to be at variance with the real interests of the Canadian people. They have spread gloom; they have breathed pessimism. They are happy only when they can revel in what is bad news for the Canadian people. When we have talked about expansion, prosperity, more jobs, their treatment has been cold water, cynicism and scorn. They do not want good news, so they go on talking about the difficulties.
There are difficulties but, Mr. Speaker, they do not need to be exaggerated, and it is no credit to hon. members opposite to have gone on in this way spreading gloom, magnifying, exaggerating, trumpeting abroad every difficulty they can conjure up. This presents real danger to the future of the Liberal party. May I say, Mr. Speaker, as a believer in the two party system, that I view this situation with very deep concern.
There have been certain criticisms in which hon. members opposite have indulged in the course of this debate, and while they are not serious I think, having introduced this budget, I should deal with them as far as time permits.
I am told first of all, Mr. Speaker, that my forecast is too optimistic. I forecast a 7 per cent increase in the gross national product over the 1958 record figure. Mr. Speaker, I put that figure forward having weighed it well; I put it forward on a solid basis, and anything that has happened in the 10 days since that figure was put before the house has gone to confirm that prognostication.
In the United States in this period respectable forecasters have come forward with

estimates that the gross national product in the United States will increase this year by between 10 and 12 per cent. We have seen in Canada in the same period a most extraordinary expansion of commercial loans. Mr. Speaker, the commercial loans in Canada amounted to $100 million last week, just about double the normal rate for this period of the year. I do not say that is going to continue at this extraordinary pace every week, but those factors are of a very great importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am satisfied that the forecast which I made of that 7 per cent increase is fully justified; and I am sure of this-and this I do not like to say, Mr. Speaker, or to find-that if this forecast is borne out in the event, the Liberals will be disappointed. They have shown that already. They will be happier, Mr. Speaker, if the recovery does not proceed as fast as I estimated in the budget speech. They do not even like to admit that there is any recovery in process. They do not want any good news. They do not want bright hopes for the Canadian economy. They prefer to dash cold water on Canadian hopes. This, Mr. Speaker, is the sorry state to which the once great Liberal party has fallen.
But when we are talking about forecasts let us go a little further in this review and test accuracy as reflected in previous figures. On June 17 last year I forecast a deficit of $648 million. As a result of further commitments undertaken later in the same session that figure was revised to $700 million. When the budget was presented to the house this year I was able to report a deficit of $616 million, and to draw the attention of the house to the fact that in our estimates of expenditures we were within two-thirds of one per cent of the amount they turned out to be. In connection with revenues, which are harder to estimate, we were in the event within 2J per cent of what the estimate had been. This combined estimate of revenues and expenditures, 1958-59, in the budget introduced on June 17, 1958, is throughout the whole post-war period, with the exception of one year, the budget which came closest to accuracy in the outcome.
Our hon. friends opposite were not very happy about this improvement in the deficit 66968-9-184
2L 1959
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming position. They were deeply stirred by it, and they have done their best since to make it appear worse. Well, Mr. Speaker, on any test the result shows, first, accuracy in the estimating and, second, an improvement in conditions in Canada since last June even over and above the anticipated improvement on which we based our estimate in the budget of 1958.
Let us look now at the record of those who are complaining now that our estimates are too optimistic. I turn to what was said by hon. gentlemen opposite in the budget debate last year. I begin naturally with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Speaking on July 3 in the budget debate and dealing with my estimate of a deficit of $648 million he said, as found at page 1902 of Hansard, "the deficit will likely be over $1 billion." Again, as found on page 1903, he said, speaking of borrowings: "Approximately $1 billion is due to government deficit." Again two months later, speaking on September 4, he said, as found on page 4574 of Hansard:
Furthermore, the huge budgetary deficit announced by the minister, which may be greater than announced by him-
And further, as found on page 4583, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) referred to a forecast by Mr. Harvey Perry, director of the Canadian tax foundation, and said that on the basis of that forecast that "our deficit would be close to $1 billion-we predicted it would go over $1 billion."
Well, Mr. Speaker, after the session the Leader of the Opposition heeded the ancient advice, "Go west, young man, go west," and west he went. He had some interesting things to say in the course of his western tour. The Winnipeg Free Press quotes him in its issue of October 6 as having said at Regina:
-"the deficit for the current year will be much greater" than the $700 million forecast by finance minister hon. Donald Fleming. . . . "My guess is that it will be close to $1 billion," Mr. Pearson said. "But that's just speculation."

There is a billion dollar deficit in a time of recession-
Well, Mr. Speaker, I made a speech in Toronto which hon. members opposite have chosen to quote very frequently since, and there I stated that in the light of the figures that were available at that time, the beginning of January, I did not think my estimate of the deficit would be very far out. Opposition leader Pearson, in a blistering attack on the government, forecast a billion dollar deficit budget "within two or three weeks".

I commend to members of the opposition the views expressed in this editorial in the Ottawa Citizen, and I ask at the same time why they chose to exaggerate and misrepresent the deficit budgeted for in 1958-59. They know and they knew when they uttered those remarks that a billion dollar deficit would have done damage


to the Canadian economy, that it would have made our fiscal position much weaker and would have exaggerated our borrowing needs. For those who would listen to them, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have brought on the Canadian economy by their talk all the harm that a billion dollar deficit would have brought upon it if they could have had their way.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a new excuse for failure.

speechtext:
They have adopted an irresponsible course, and they have convicted themselves.
They have also had something to say to us, if you please, about promises. I wish to deal with what has been said by them about promises. With respect to the subject of tax reduction in 1957, the Prime Minister and others associated with him in the campaign said that if the people would give the Prime Minister a mandate we would bring about a reduction in taxes. The people elected us and we carried out our promise. In December, 1957 the government introduced substantial reductions in taxation aggregating at that time $178 million, reductions that took various forms; increases in the exemptions for dependent children, reductions in the rates of taxation on those in the lowest income brackets, an increase in the portion of corporate income that is exempt in order to benefit small corporations. Hon. members opposite had a much better opportunity than we did to bring about reductions of this kind because times were better in 1955, 1956 and 1957.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But even in the face of their opportunities they chose not to reduce taxes and we, grappling as we were with the difficult conditions they left us heir to, brought about reductions in taxation.
We had another election campaign in 1958. Already we were spending very heavily to combat a recession. In the campaign we did not make promises of general tax reductions under these circumstances. We pointed to several individual reductions which, if the people would re-elect us, we would bring about; and we did. This parliament was elected on March 31, 1958 and the promises on which the Conservatives were elected in the majority in this house have been carried out and will continue to be carried out.
In June of last year we proceeded to carry out those promises we had made that we would bring about certain individual reductions in taxation. We brought in a new estates tax act which reduced the tax on smaller estates. We reduced the sales taxes on purchases by municipalities and brought about a number of other individual reductions

which aggregated $26 million. Mr. Speaker, the aggregate of the reductions made in 1957 and 1958 totalled $202 million, under the circumstances then existing. But under the circumstances of today, in the light of conditions of today, the numbers of taxpayers, incomes and so on, these reductions have been estimated by my department to be worth not $202 million but $230 million per year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Inflation.

I have said that that promise of ours was fulfilled. That promise was fulfilled to the letter.
I draw attention to the fact that again in this budget, Mr. Speaker, we have demonstrated, as we did in 1957 and 1958, the same concern for the man of small means, the small taxpayer and small businessman. The present budget removes from them much of the burden of the increases. Today we are showing that same concern for the person of small means. This has been accompanied, Mr. Speaker, by the largest program of aid to provinces, municipalities, hospital insurance, house construction, hospital construction, social security and aid to employment in the history of Canada. This is the answer to the double talk we have heard for years from hon. members opposite about the big interests. Our proven concern has been for the people of small means in this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, they talk about reduced expenditures. Certainly before we came into office we inveighed against waste and extravagance and the expenses of government under the Liberal administration. We had reason for doing so. If we had been elected earlier unquestionably we could have saved this country money by eliminating waste and extravagance. In the 1957 campaign we asked the people for a mandate to increase social security expenditures and aid to the provinces and municipalities. We were given that mandate and we have carried out our promises. We never promised or pretended that these increases in social security could be carried out without somebody paying for them. In 1957-58 we had to work with the budget that had already been brought in by the Liberals, on the strength of which the spending programs of that year were already launched and commitments made before we came into office in late June, 1957.
In the 1958 campaign we promised the people that while continuing our social security program and proceeding with and hastening the introduction of hospital insurance programs and spending heavily and constructively to combat unemployment, we would continue to wage war against waste and extravagance. We have done so, and we shall continue to do so wherever we find 66968-9-184J

The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming them. The treasury board this year has been tighter and closer in its scrutiny of estimates than ever before. A lot of these things are not talked about in detail everywhere, but let there be no doubt about it; the treasury board today is doing an effective piece of work. There are not going to be any more printing bureau scandals; there are not going to be any more of these spring-filled dance floors. There is a tightening of the rein on expenditures.
When we are told about the expansion of the civil service, may I remind you that in bringing in the estimates for the present year, on February 5, I drew attention at page 706 of Hansard to these facts. I said:
Notwithstanding the increases of $42 million in salaries and wages and pay and allowances, there has been no appreciable expansion in the strength of the civil service of Canada or of the defence forces. While additional responsibilities have been assumed, the over-all increase in the size of the government establishment for 1959-60 will be only .4 per cent over 1958-59. This is the smallest annual growth shown since 1951. It demonstrates the government's continuing effort to increase efficiency and at the same time to economize on the use of staff.
It is appropriate that at this point I should ask hon. members opposite if they will be frank with the house and the Canadian people. Do you want to reduce old age pensions? Do you want to eliminate hospital insurance? Do you want to reduce or eliminate the expenditures we are making on housing, on public works, on our winter works program and other measures to combat unemployment? Would you deny the aid we are giving to the provinces and municipalities? I put on Hansard on the evening of April 9 table No. 1 which shows the rapidly increasing assistance we are giving to the provinces of this country. This table did not escape the attention of one Liberal journal in this country, and I should like to quote a sentence or two from an editorial appearing in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of April 17. I find this:
But the tax-sharing agreements aside, the provincial administrations have received from the federal treasury a good deal more financial assistance since the Conservatives took office. This fact is usually overlooked but Finance Minister Fleming brought it into prominence during his recent budget speech. He made public a most interesting table which, if nothing else, seems to prove the federal government has been quite generous with the 10 provincial governments, generally speaking.
There are further statements in that interesting editorial to the same effect. I commend it to the attention of hon. members opposite. So, Mr. Speaker, I ask hon. members opposite where they would reduce expenditures, if they say expenditures should be reduced? We are paying the provinces

The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming this year, as table 1 shows, as compared with last year, $148 million more in these various ways. Our responsibilities for social security and pensions of all kinds are increased in this budget over last year by another $148 million. Here is where the increases in 1959-60 estimated expenditures lie as compared with 1958-59.
You do not hear frank statements of that kind from hon. members opposite. So I say, Mr. Speaker, we have had from hon. members opposite, while they have been mouthing these phrases about reduced expenditures, not one word, not a single proposal, for taking one cent off the expenditures in this year's estimates. On the contrary, one of them has come forward with a proposal that would probably increase expenditures this year by substantially over $100 million.
They say something now about a balanced budget. I have something to say to them about that too, Mr. Speaker. We did not promise, when we went to the people, that we would balance the budget this year. We did not promise that we would balance the budget last year. A balanced budget, as such, was not even mentioned in the course of the 1958 election campaign. We were not elected on any promise or any platform that for last year or this year or any other particular year we would balance the budget. Nowhere in the 1958 campaign can any such assurance or promise on our part be found. I give that denial, to put it mildly, directly to the kind of nonsense and rot to which we have been listening from hon. members opposite in recent days.
Sir, we did hear something from the Liberals previously on this subject. Perhaps it is time, now, to turn to something interesting they have said. They talk to us in this amendment about deficit financing. Mr. Speaker, here are the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) spoken in the house in the last budget debate as reported on page 1898 of Hansard for July 3:
Therefore it is not the deficit as such that we are criticizing, because deficits are required in the kind of situation we have in this country at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, that expression has never been withdrawn. Who are those who talk today about deficit financing? We had some other interesting comments which fell from the lips of the Leader of the Opposition in the course of the election campaign, and not once but several times. I recall to mind one in particular on February 10, 1958, when he said that the Liberals would bring about a tax reduction immediately of $400 million. That was followed up on March 21 in Toronto with a promise of a $100 million tax holiday. That is an aggregate of $500 million. This tax holiday
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) .1
is an interesting thing because the people were going to be given a tax holiday, if the Liberals were elected, right after the election, and when this brief tax holiday was over up would bound the same old rates of taxation again, like a bouncing rubber ball or my hon. friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate (Mr. Pickersgill).
Mr. Speaker, for hon. members opposite to charge us with bad faith when we made no such statement to the Canadian people in the election campaign is to indulge in the sort of thing they like to accuse others of, namely making false and misleading statements. I just point out in passing on this subject of deficits that if the Liberals, with their tax holiday and policy of deficit financing, had been in office and carried out their election promises, their deficit today for the fiscal year 1958-59 would be twice as much as ours was. Certainly it would have been well over a billion dollars and probably closer to one and a quarter billion dollars.
I see my time is running short, and I have not as much time as I would have wished to answer all the new attacks we have heard in this house with regard to certain forms of accounting. As regards the defence replacement account I have time only to say that this account has been in existence now for some years, actually nine years, and for eight of those years the Liberals did the budgeting. In seven of those eight years they provided drawdowns from the defence replacement account and they were used to improve their budget position. But there is a difference between the Liberal methods and ours. They did not tell the House of Commons what they were doing. We did. We told the House of Commons beforehand, expressly and frankly, that what we were doing was in the interest of better accounting to parliament. So we did what was right and proper and what we said we would do and what parliament last year approved. We have wiped out that defence replacement account.
They also complain about the old age security fund. How they have forgotten, Mr. Speaker, that the old age security fund was to be on a pay as you go basis. That was what the committee recommended in 1951. That was what Mr. Abbott brought before the house and is the system which came into effect on January 1, 1952. That is what the act calls for. It lays on the Minister of Finance the responsibility for making recommendations in this respect. Mr. Speaker, it has escaped the recollection of hon. members opposite, but what has happened in all these years? In 1951-52 the act was in force only three months and the deficit of $50 million was charged to general budgetary expenditure. In 1952-53 the deficit of $100 million was covered by

a temporary loan; it was not charged up against the budget of that year. That loan was written off as charged against the reserve for losses on realization of assets in 1953-54, and was not charged as a budgetary expenditure, and I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Abbott did not want that shown in his budget.
But hon. members opposite, having forgotten that they were party to that act in 1953-54, now say, when we put this fund on a sound basis and propose that the deficit for this year should be borne in succeeding years, that that is all wrong. How do they account for the fact that in 1953-54 they charged the deficit for 1952-53 up against, not the budget -it did not appear in the budget-but one of those convenient reserves which they had tucked away in the consolidated revenue fund where things were not intended to show. So in a variety of ways since then they have gone on.
They do not have to take my word as to our solution. I would like to read from the Toronto Star, the issue of April 10, 1959, and let hon. members know what is said about this budget:
It is time to put the old age pension fund on a self-sustaining basis-contributions fell $184 million short of disbursements last year. And Mr. Fleming proposes to do it in an even-handed way, raising the levy on personal income, corporation income and the sales tax from 2 to 3 per cent each.
He has also dealt fairly in raising personal and corporation income taxes by 2 per cent. The increases apply only to the top income fifth of individuals and companies; obviously the ones best able to pay more. Nor do we think there can be any serious quarrel with his modest tax increases on liquor and cigarettes.
That is the Liberal Toronto Star speaking.

speechtext:
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming
I draw attention, however, to what is either an accidental or a calculated confusion in the minds and speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite. They talk about this rise in interest rates which reflects the extent to which the Canadian bond market is affected by conditions in the United States, and they confuse what is happening now, or what has been happening in relation to interest rates, with what happened under the Liberal government under what has come to be known as the tight money policy of the Liberals. Mr. Speaker, here is the essence of the difference: on our part, we have done what we could, in the light of the difficulties of the situation, to resist the pressures which have caused an increase in interest rates on this continent; but in the case of the Liberal government, the rise in interest rates and the other things they did were brought about in pursuance of deliberate government policy. There is the difference. Their policy was designed deliberately to check business expansion and interest rates were pushed up as part of that policy.
But that was not the only form which that policy took; part of that policy was intended to bring about, deliberately, a severe contraction in commercial credit and to force the banks to cut back on credit, and we well know the way in which the application of that policy harmed business, particularly small business, farmers and others. We opposed and we denounced that tight money policy, and we were right, and the Canadian people at the polls vindicated our stand in regard to the excesses of the Liberal government in deliberately pursuing that policy as they did. And, to the limit of our powers as a government, when we took office we reversed that policy and set about undoing the mischief that that policy had done in retarding the Canadian economy. Therefore, at this time, we are not in the position that tight money conditions have been brought about by the government of the day, as was the case when the Leader of the Opposition was a member of the government.

speechtext:
Hon. members of this house will see clearly that there is a world of difference between the policies of this government and the policies pursued by that discredited Liberal government which was dismissed from office and upon which the Canadian people passed a second verdict, on March 31, 1958, a verdict which has left them in the unhappy position in which they find themselves today.
So, Mr. Speaker, I have dealt with the terms of this extraordinary amendment, an amendment which has the temerity to accuse this government of having made promises which it did not make; of having been elected on the basis of promises which it did not give during the election campaign, and of having broken promises which it did not make.
We were not elected on any such platform as hon. members opposite have talked about. I have gone over the record of the 1958 campaign, and I have shown how wildly inaccurate have been the statements of hon. members opposite about our platform and our program as laid before the Canadian people at that time. The bad faith which is to be found in relation to this debate is not in the budget; it is not in the proposals to which the budget speech led. The bad faith lies in the unfounded charges that are contained in the opposition amendment. I suppose we might leave it at that. The opposition has nothing to offer. They did not have anything of which they thought sufficiently highly to be worth according even an honourable mention in their amendment. Such be their verdict upon themselves.
I do not propose to review now what I said in the budget speech which was, I realize, of quite excessive length. But this may be said for the budget which is now under consideration, that it is based upon a view of the present situation which frankly takes account of the difficulties as well as of the bright spots, and faces those difficulties and prescribes clear courses of action, if the house will approve, for meeting those difficulties. It states the tax policy of the government, and states it clearly. It is a constructive effort. It contains a group of constructive proposals based upon a realistic approach to the problems. I think it may be fair to say that it is an approach which will, if approved by the house, contribute substantially to recovery. If it be optimistic, it is optimistic with good reason to be optimistic. It applies what I believe to be a sound principle in dealing

with economic conditions that are changing as rapidly as economic conditions have changed in the period of the last year. It uses the fiscal methods open to the government as a flexible means of meeting the problems which confront us at this time.
It may well be that this budget does mark a very important point in the developing economy of this period. I feel complimented indeed by the article written by Mr. Bruce Hutchison, who by all accounts is an eminent Liberal, in what he has had to say about the budget. I have here his article which is headed, "Budget Shows Double Courage", and which concludes with this statement which I should like to leave with the house:
If so, the budget may be judged later as one of the most important in our history.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether that statement will be borne out in the light of events. I am not going to make claims of that kind but I am going to say that this is a realistic budget and one based upon a policy and not, like the amendment, which is based on a lack of policy. We have kept our promises. We shall continue to keep our promises. Because this amendment falsely accuses the government in this respect we ask the house to reject the amendment and reject it decisively.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that many hon. members in this house must feel almost drowned by the verbiage that has flowed from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) during the last 53 minutes. My regret is that so much verbosity should have come from a cabinet minister and particularly the Minister of Finance containing no logic or reasoning.
The minister opened his remarks by informing the house that he has become philosophic and relaxed. Philosophy and relaxation are good in their place, if correct, but I personally have no hesitation in saying that the philosophy which I fear the minister has now adopted is not in the best interests of this country. In his budget speech and again this afternoon he made it evident that his philosophy is to close his eyes to the realities of conditions in Canada and he chooses to be relaxed at a time when there are major problems requiring attention and solution.
It was delightful from an oratorical point of view to listen for 53 minutes to Don Fleming Quixote charging against mirages to the loud huzzas of his colleagues.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not so very loud.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At this time Canada needs as minister of finance something more than a Don Quixote charging at mirages. We need
The Budget-Mr. Winch a minister who will face economic realities and problems that cannot be solved by excessive verbiage or emotional eloquence or by charges levied against other individuals or parties. We need someone who will face the realities of increasing interest rates and continuing unemployment and who will find solutions for problems relating to the export markets required by this country. These matters require a true philosopher and realist, not a Quixote.
The Minister of Finance referred to prophecies respecting increased gross national products in both Canada and the United States. This is something to which we look forward. It was very noticeable, however, that in the budget speech and in his remarks this afternoon when the minister spoke of increases in the gross national product he did not relate the increases to the value of the dollar. Therein lies one of the fallacies in the approach and prognostications of the minister.
It was also noticeable that when approximately twenty minutes ago the minister nearly burst his buttons telling us that in 1957 he had reduced taxation by $178 million we did not hear him say a confounded word about the fact that in 1958 he increased it by $325 million. Apparently from the minister's point of view there are some things to be emphasized and others to be ignored or given not too much emphasis.
The minister made some comment about a stringent economy but I think it should be noted that although we have no legislation concerning social welfare on the order paper this session the minister this year is asking for an expenditure of $350 million more than was requested in the budget last year.
During the 53 minutes the minister consumed this afternoon he continued the sham battle between the government and official opposition. I believe we have had enough of sham battles and charges and countercharges between the government and official opposition concerning what they said they would do and what they actually did.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you sorry he mentioned only two parties?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We do not utilize the time of this house engaging in idle chatter of that kind. I could spend my entire time making similar statements, charges and accusations but I shall not do so because I do not believe in talking simply for the sake of talking nor do I countenance unnecessary repetition. Enough has been said concerning campaign promises and the fulfilment or lack of fulfilment of those promises.
I wish to tell the minister that I think he fell down in the policy decisions he made

The Budget-Mr. Winch relative to taxation. I know that hon. members of the government attempt to advance the argument that it is not taxation that is going to hit the average citizen in Canada. We say that such an assertion definitely is not correct. When an increase of 1 per cent in sales tax is introduced by the government the government is delving into the pocket of every individual in Canada.
I say to that that I find it difficult to understand why the Minister of Finance, when he is getting his greatest revenue mainly from the average citizen of Canada, feels he has to hit them more. I have reference, of course, to the increase on cigarettes. Before the last increase in taxation appeared cigarettes paid a federal tax of 17.7 cents on a package of 20, which I understand is 54 per cent of the retail price. Because the great majority of the average citizens enjoy their smoke and when the government is receiving 17.7 cents on a package of 20, 54 per cent of the retail price, I say it is a darned shame that the minister finds it necessary or decides to add an additional two cents per package of 20. What I say about it being a darned shame I also apply to the increase in spirituous liquors.
Prior to the federal tax increase approximately 80 cents out of every dollar spent on the retail price of spirituous liquors went to the federal and provincial governments. If my understanding and analysis are correct, the federal government receives 43 cents out of every dollar spent. Now, of course, it is going to be more. I personally want to tell the Minister of Finance that when he is already getting 43 cents out of every dollar spent on spirituous liquor I think he is just putting on a little bit too much pressure when he wants still more money. It would not be so bad if he would bring in a law to take some of the water out of it; but since he is still going to levy his tax on the amount of water in the spirituous liquor, then I say 43 cents out of every dollar is enough without an additional 12 cents a bottle. I have to say that I am grateful for one thing, namely that he has left the workingman's beer alone. The 1 per cent is going to have some effect, but I pay my compliments to the brewers who have already announced that they will absorb the sales tax increase.
In view of the fact that the Minister of Finance has found it necessary to increase taxation so as to raise approximately an additional $325 million, I feel the increases he has announced would have been more acceptable, more reasonable and more logical if he first of all, or at the same time, had gone after those who make millions and pay no taxes at all. I refer to corporation and company promoters and stock manipulators

who, of course on the evidence, in Ontario alone invest a few hundred dollars and make millions.
Every endeavour that we have made in the estimates committee to find out whether or not the government collects any taxes has been turned down. Therefore, there are only two men who know whether or not those who make money out of stock promotions- since they are in the know-pay anything in income tax. I refer to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) who refused to give information in the estimates committee, and the Minister of Finance. I say to the Minister of Finance, if you are going to hit the people of this country for more than 17.7 cents per package of 20 cigarettes and more than 43 cents out of every dollar spent on spirituous liquors, then why have you not the common decency to collect something from those who make millions and pay no taxes whatsoever? Any demand by the Minister of Finance for increased taxation on the common people will be better understood if he will interest himself in going to those who in the past and now pay no taxes on certain financial manipulations in Canada.
I was most interested yesterday when the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) addressed this house in this debate. The hon. member had this to say, as reported at page 2841 of Hansard. He was speaking of the Minister of Finance:
I believe that already his performance in this most onerous office in these most difficult times rates him with the great finance ministers of our nation's history, men like Fielding, Sir Thomas White and E. M. Rhodes.
The hon. member for Queens is most certainly entitled to his opinion; so are we all; so am I. The Minister of Finance, in introducing his budget and informing this house and the country of the taxation increases did not deal with many of the realities and problems we are facing; did not make any statement whatsoever of policy or legislation to collect millions from those who pay no taxes now. I think the hon. member for Queens was wrong. The Minister of Finance will not go down in history as a great finance minister, as was intimated by the hon. member for Queens. In my opinion he will go down as "the great betrayer" because in his budget this year he has done three things. He divorced financial policy this year from his own government's and party's campaign promises. He divorced himself and his government from a realistic taxation policy; and he divorced financial policy from the needs of the common citizens. It is for these three reasons that I say he should be, and I think will be, eventually known as "the great betrayer".

I have mentioned the word "divorce" three times. From now on in the 20 minutes I still have at my disposal I am not going to discuss the budget because I have no intention of repeating the statements and the arguments which have already been put forward in the past by previous speakers. I should like to discuss the question of divorce because this debate gives me the opportunity to discuss not only the budget itself but anything else I feel to be of importance and should be discussed in the House of Commons. I recognize that in so doing I am raising a most controversial subject but I do feel it is necessary to speak upon it from two points of view; one, the handling of divorce for the provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec through the medium of the Senate and the House of Commons; and, two the matter of the law as it relates to divorce itself.
Before I enter into these two subjects I want to make it very clear that I am not expressing C.C.F. national policy nor am I giving voice to any policy of the C.C.F. members in this house. I am speaking strictly from a personal point of view on two matters which I feel should be brought to the attention of the house and be given consideration by the government and the house in the not too distant future.
Section 91 of the British North America Act of 1867 gives to the parliament of Canada exclusive legislative jurisdiction in relation to marriage and divorce. All provinces in our country except two have courts that deal with divorces. The provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec do not have such courts. As a result, the Senate and the House of Commons find themselves in the position of having to deal with matters which actually should not come before members of parliament for investigation and decision.
A great deal has been said in the house in the past about the extraordinary situation that faces members of the House of Commons in having to sit in judgment on divorce cases. Over the years suggestions have been made that separate courts should be established for these two provinces or that the Exchequer Court of Canada should handle divorce cases from Quebec and Newfoundland. It is quite evident, however, that no move is contemplated to establish outside courts in order to remove from the Senate and the House of Commons the responsibility of dealing with matters of divorce. Because there is no indication that such a step will be taken, I am taking it on myself to throw out a suggestion different from the establishment of courts but one which I think is worthy of consideration and
The Budget-Mr. Winch will remove from the House of Commons the unhealthy task which up till now it has had to accept.
In conversation with constitutional authorities I have found that parliament has the right to delegate power and as a result I want to make a suggestion which I ask members to think about calmly and reasonably. I suggest that we establish a precedent and that the House of Commons and the Senate should pass an act under which the Senate shall have the power to deal with divorce cases, royal assent then being given by resolution, so that the Senate alone will exercise the power preceding royal assent now required of both houses of parliament.
I say that if the United Kingdom can say that certain bills passed by the house of commons need not be passed by the house of lords and shall become acts on receiving royal assent then the opposite is true if the procedure is authorized by both houses.
In putting this proposal forward it is my personal opinion that it would be beneficial because divorce bills would no longer need to be considered on the floor of the House of Commons. I believe that the prestige of the Senate would be enhanced if sole jurisdiction were conferred upon it in this regard. I say that our present system is clumsy and outmoded and that the procedure I recommend would greatly simplify the situation. I say further that the Senate has the time and has developed the necessary machinery.
I recognize that there are three possible arguments against my suggestion. First, it might be said that it would saddle the Senate with the whole problem of divorce. I admit that but the Senate is already saddled with the problem so there is nothing new there. Second, it is also arguable that the participation of the commons in divorce bills is a useful check on Senate. In my opinion this argument is not sustainable. I should like to give the house statistics to substantiate that contention. I am certain that the members of the house who are present will be interested in this information.
From 1945 through 1958 the Senate committee heard 4,126 divorce petitions. Of these the Senate committee rejected 54. That meant that the House of Commons received 4,072 divorce bills from 1945 through 1958. The House of Commons rejected 18. There may be some members who would prefer to have information for the last two or three years. From 1956 through 1958 the Senate committee heard 1,219 divorce petitions and rejected 20. Therefore during the same period the House of Commons received 1,199 divorce bills. The House of Commons rejected four.
It is quite obvious that the House of Commons does not sit as a court on divorce bills.
2896	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Winch In the light of the fact that out of 4,072 divorce bills received by the house from 1945 through 1958 only 18 were rejected and in the period from 1956 through 1958 only four were rejected, we are making a farce of the procedure.
I come now to the main argument that can be used against my proposal. It can be reasonably argued that such an idea would involve an abdication or abandonment of the powers of parliament. I recognize that. I recognize what kind of a precedent it would be. But I feel that this objection can be met by pointing out that the act would be passed by both houses of parliament and if found unworkable or too shackling it could be repealed or amended by a subsequent act in any future parliament.
I should like to spend more time on the matter of our procedure but I am not going to do so. I hope I have given enough information to justify honest consideration by the government and by all members of the house with regard to the procedure of handling divorces from Newfoundland and Quebec by the two houses of parliament. I say that if the government is not prepared to do as I think it should, if it is not prepared to take the necessary steps to remove this work now required of both houses by referring it to an outside or already established court, then the government should have the guts at least to give consideration to the type of proposal I have made this afternoon.
It is not sufficient, at least in my opinion, to speak about the procedure of divorce in two provinces, without also saying a few words about the law of divorce in Canada. This, too, is a highly controversial subject. I get into trouble sometimes because I insist on raising highly controversial issues. I feel that if something should be said, then it is going to be said; that is, if I think it is right.
I do say on behalf of the minority-I am happily married myself, so I am not concerned-that Canada has the most antedated and antiquated divorce laws. Canada's divorce laws are more backward than those of most countries in this world.
Time and time again in my capacity as a representative of my constituency in this house, and previously in the provincial legislature, I have met persons who had real problems. They have been deserted for years, and where the husband or wife is they do not know; nobody knows. If a woman is deserted for a period of years, why should that woman be denied the normal happiness of life, the normal expressions of life? Should we insist that she become immoral by living as a common law wife? I do not believe so. When we have a person subjected to


physical cruelty and sexual cruelty, why does the law say that that person must remain tied to such an individual? Why is it that when a person is committed to an insane asylum and found incurably insane the spouse must be denied the right to a normal life? Why is it that when a man is committed to jail as a sexual psychopath-I understand that term is going to be changed-or as a habitual criminal or is found guilty of murder and the sentence commuted to life imprisonment, the spouse should be denied a normal life?
I ask that the members of this house and the government just think these things over. I am not alone in this opinion. I was most interested in reading in a local newspaper the other day a report from Vancouver which said that the British Columbia churches now advocate easier divorce. It says that five of seven British Columbia presbyteries of the United Church of Canada have advocated broader grounds for divorce, and then outline what they think should be the broader grounds. I know you realize, Mr. Speaker, as we all do, that marriage is a sacred and wonderful thing, and everything possible should be done to maintain a marriage, especially when there are children. But under the circumstances I have outlined, why should we in Canada be so far behind the rest of the world, be so unchristian and heathenish, as to deny happiness and a full life to those who are caught in certain circumstances.
As a result of my own personal reading, my consultations with many members of the church, social welfare organizations and as a result of my talks with individuals caught in the web of circumstances, I should like to recommend certain changes. I have no hesitation when I speak on this matter in giving my own views. Let me make this clear; the spouse would have to ask for the divorce because if there was a desire to wait and hope that the person would come out of the insane asylum or out of jail, then that would be the responsibility of the spouse. I should like to recommend that the divorce law be changed; and in addition to the existing grounds for divorce, the following be added: Desertion for three years; after repeated physical and sexual cruelty; after insanity for three years if the spouse is still retained in an institution; and, if one is incarcerated in a penal institution with a sentence over five years or an indefinite sentence after serving a definite sentence of three years.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that I first had a few words to say about what the Minister of Finance said on the budget and then on two matters which I did not think anyone else would raise, and which I felt should be raised. Having done so, I

would ask the government and every member of the House of Commons to search their own minds, their own consciences, and not only answer the questions which I am about to ask but also decide whether or not they feel they have a part to play in solving the problems of the minority, who have the same right to happiness as the majority. The question I should like to ask is this: Under what code of human behaviour, religious ethic, or civilized law should the innocent suffer for the sins of the guilty? That is what our law imposes upon people today. I leave the answer to that question to the thinking and the decency of the government and the members of this house.
