the second reading of Bill No. C-ll, to amend the Canada Elections Act (publication of straw poll results).
He said: In introducing this amendment to the Canada Elections Act we are asking for the prohibition of the publication of opinion polls or what is commonly called straw polls prior to an election. These polls have been given pseudo-recognition by the people of Canada as being fair, being honest, though the integrity of opinion polls was questioned as recently as 1948 in a very large example.
The Canadian electors are in no way assured that the polls are representative or that the questions which are asked are representative questions. A question asked sometimes of an unrepresentative group leads to an answer which is occasionally used by political parties during the elections. Opinion polls are being conducted in the major portion of our schools. There are many advantages to conducting these polls. For one thing, it keeps a large number of people employed who are operating private polls of one type or another. Second, I think it is a good thing to discuss at election time who the pupil would vote for and probably the reason why that pupil would so vote. But on a number of occasions it has been very easy to tell prior to an election exactly what people in a certain area will do, because their children, attending school and reporting through their polls, make this information available to the teacher.
For some odd reason, possibly a quirk, of the Canadian mind, quite often our people
Canada Elections Act
have a tendency to accept these polls and decide that they have to vote in an election for the party that is going to win. So it sometimes gives an unfair impetus to the recipient of a very favourable poll. There would be nothing wrong with this if polls were conducted in a manner which would assure the people reading the answers that the polls were an honest sampling of opinion and that the questions had been designed to give true answers and were reported in that manner. But I do not think this is always true.
In the last few months we have seen where polls have been conducted and have not been accepted by the federal government. This is probably more evident in the Department of Labour than in any other federal department. The dominion bureau of statistics operates on the principle of the sample poll. I do not think any member in this house could tell who did the sampling for the department. I never came in contact with anybody who was ever asked any of the questions, but it was found that the system being used was not necessarily the most efficient one which could be developed, and within the last few months the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has been using a number of other methods to find out the number of people seeking employment in Canada. This being one of our official polls it would indicate that it does not even operate in the manner in which we wish it to operate.
If the polls were supervised and the questions standardized, and use of these questions by correspondents and newspapers was made to give a fair sampling of opinion, then there would be less objection to them. But this is not the case. In the United States election of 1948 it was a well-known fact that a number of the polls in that country were so conducted that the questions were asked in such a manner as to receive a particular answer.
This information has been very difficult to come by, because after a poll is conducted and the results published nobody ever looks back on it again. So we tend to forget where the polls made mistakes in the past and are much more interested in what the poll is going to report on the new problem which has arisen. British Columbia faced this matter in 1939 when they passed section 168 of the British Columbia elections act, which reads:
No person, corporation or organization shall after the issue of the writ for any election take any straw vote, which will prior to the election distinguish the political opinions of the voters in any electoral district.
In moving this amendment we are not suggesting that these polls do not be taken, because they do serve some purpose. We

Canada Elections Act
are only suggesting that the results of the polls be not published during the period of election, or from the time the writ has been issued until the time the election itself is conducted.
In 1948 the matter of how honest and trustworthy polls were was shown in an election when Mr. Truman and Mr. Dewey were fighting for the presidency of the United States. Mr. Truman was fighting an election for the third time, but there were many reasons why his popularity should have decreased. He, through congress, had suggested that several things be done which were not too popular, and a number of the pollsters in that country were pledged to support, and to elect if possible, Mr. Dewey, and they worked toward that end. Very little information has ever been available as to what polls have accomplished or with regard to their operation, but a little book was written by Morris L. Ernst and David Loth called "The People Know Best. The Ballots vs. the Polls". It contains some observations which I think are interesting enough to examine. It points out at page 11:
The presidential election of 1948 has given us the most dramatic, the most significant example of the hazards which our basic concept is facing. With a unanimity which has seldom been equalled in our political history, the men and women upon whom we relied for facts, for comment and for opinion were hypnotized (or hynotized themselves) into the conviction that President Harry S. Truman's campaign was hopeless.
The great damage to our way of life was not that they were wrong. Far more serious is the attitude of all of us toward that error. We laughed at the recollection of their pontifical certainties. We sneered at their motives, at their intelligence, at the validity of their information, at their methods and at the media through which they spoke to us. We were gleeful or sad over their discomfiture, depending upon how the results of the election pleased us. But there is also an opportunity for us to gain a more substantial benefit. We can use our experience of this great illusion to improve our media of information and our understanding of them.
Then it goes on to say that this is one of the things that we must be on guard against today, because if we are not we are going to allow the pollsters to form an opinion and thus develop our need for voting in one direction because we want to be on the winning side, rather than being able to decide for ourselves which is right and which is wrong. This book points out that in many cases it does take away from the voter the right to make up his own mind and establish for himself his own opinion. Some of the polls in that election in 1948 gave Dewey 96 per cent of the vote, while others gave only as high as 56.

I think it is interesting to note some of the questions which are asked. In one of the Gallup poll ballots appears this statement:
The battle for control of Congress in the November election will be far more closely fought than the presidential battle-
As you feel today, would you be more likely to vote for the Democratic or for the Republican candidate for congress from your district?
The question which is asked does not relate, hon. members will notice, to the statement which precedes it. And then the result is reported as a Gallup poll report, as follows:
Democratic candidate	 41%
Republican candidate	 41
Other parties	 l
No opinion	 17
Another question was asked on August 12, and again a statement was made in connection with it, as follows:
Although congress brushed aside President Truman's request for limited price controls, there has been a sharp increase of public sentiment in favour of controls since the special Congressional session was called-
Do you think the government should or should not put back rationing and price controls on some products?
And the answer which was given, reads:
Should	 56%
Should not	 35
Price controls but	not rationing	 2
No opinion	 7
When these results are reported in the newspapers an impression is created that the issue has already been decided in the minds of the majority of the electorate. I suggest that this type of poll taking is not accurate, and that it is not necessarily honest. It is to the credit of the people of the United States that they saw fit in that election to vote on the basis of their own opinions rather than accept the opinion reached by most of the news commentators and all the public opinion polls.
All this, in my opinion, establishes a case for prohibiting the conducting of this type of poll and the reporting of these polls in the press during elections, because the use of these methods is eliminating one of the basic rights which the people possess-the right of choice. We depend a great deal on statistics, on publications and on facts and figures which are used as yardsticks, among them, for example, the figures which are published every month with regard to the cost of living. Publications of this kind are taken as facts and are accepted by the people as being facts. If we publish opinion polls as facts in the same way people will tend to use them and depend on them as crutches rather than to find out for themselves.
I would very much appreciate a vote on this matter. We have 31 public bills and orders

on the order paper; we have spent one day on each one of them, and have achieved no results. I am not sure whether hon. members are in favour of the proposal I am making or not, but 1 have noticed in the last few weeks that many people are in favour of it. Yet we still take the whole hour, and then defeat the measure by letting it go by the board. I strongly urge the government to allow a number of these 31 items to be voted on. They are all important to the people who put them on the order paper and there are a number which are a good deal more important than the one in which I am interested at the present time. I appeal to the government either to oppose this measure or to speak in its favour through one of its representatives, and thus allow us to continue with other matters. Otherwise I suggest we might as well discontinue the item of public bills altogether, because I think we would be wasting a great deal of time on these subjects.

speechtext:
think this bill is a foot-in-the-door infringement against freedom of expression, freedom of opinion and freedom of the press. Indeed, it is an insult to the Canadian people and I, for one, if there is a vote, will vote against it. What right have we to sit here in this House of Commons and legislate against expressions of opinion from the Canadian people, published or otherwise? What right have we to say that the Canadian people must not be allowed to read about the opinions of their fellow countrymen?
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), in what I think was an attitude of arrogant superiority, is saying that the Canadian people cannot be trusted to think for themselves, and, furthermore, that we must protect them from the thoughts of others. This bill says to the Canadian people; you are so colourless, so opinionless, that we cannot trust you to read about the opinions of other people. I do think this is an insult to the Canadian people. One moment the socialists are viewing the situation with alarm
Canada Elections Act
because they say the polls are influencing voting, and the next moment, still viewing the situation with alarm, they are saying that the polls are not infallible and that- as the hon. member for Timiskaming himself pointed out-the polls were in fact wrong in 1948 and President Truman did win the election in the United States. Moreover, the polls did not seem to influence voting in the 1957 Canadian election.
I say that the socialists cannot have it both ways. They cannot say that the polls influence voting while maintaining at the same time that the polls can be wrong and, therefore, do not influence voting. I think that public opinion polls are part of our democracy, and not only of our democracy; in 15 countries around the world these polls are taken. I should just like to put the names of a few of these countries on record, because there is a certain significance attached to them. They include Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Denmark, Sweden, Italy, Holland and Norway. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that none of these countries are communist countries. Communism will not allow the publication or expression of opinions. I do not suppose communist leaders even want to hear about public opinion as expressed in public opinion polls. Or perhaps, like the socialists, they are afraid of public opinion.
The passing of this bill would, I feel, place Canada in a ludicrous position. It would certainly indicate that Canadian politicians are afraid of public opinion, and I believe that to legislate against the publication of polls would be to legislate against freedom of opinion. I do not know how the hon. member for Timiskaming who professes to believe in a bill of rights can reconcile this bill to such a belief.
How far would such a censorship as this go? What about those who go across the country just before an election and who, normally, in the course of their work, comment on the state of public opinion? Practically every large newspaper sends reporters across the country to make surveys and take polls, and these reports are subsequently published in the newspapers. Is the hon. member suggesting that they should be censored, too, or that they should be made illegal? In my opinion he is, because the amendment begins with the words:
No person, company or corporation shall publish results of straw polls-
I think this is dangerous and evil legislation even to contemplate. Not only is it menacing freedom of opinion but freedom of the press.

Canada Elections Act
In his explanatory note the hon. member for Timiskaming sets down the purpose of his amendment to the Canada Elections Act in these words:
The purpose of this amendment is to prohibit, and to make punishable as an illegal practice, the publication in any manner before election day of the results of a straw vote or poll of the political opinions of the electors.
We are told that that is the purpose of this bill. What the hon. member has not told us is the real reason for the presentation of this bill. I suggest that the true reason is that the socialists are afraid of public opinion and perhaps with justification because public opinion and public favour certainly have not been very heartily on their side in the last few elections.
Last year when the hon. member for Timiskaming introduced this same bill in the house, as reported at page 2831 of Hansard of July 29, 1958 he had this to say:
We all know of cases where questions are asked of the general public which are very innocent in nature but by the time the results of such polls are used by certain advertising agencies and implications are drawn from them, the information presented to the public does not necessarily represent the opinions expressed by the participants in the poll.
I do not understand this strange generalization. The hon. member concluded that statement by saying:
There is actually no guarantee to the Canadian people that such polls are taken on a regular sample basis-
What does the hon. member mean when he suggests that all of us know of cases where innocent questions are asked and implications drawn which do not represent the opinions expressed by those polled? I for one know of no such cases. I can see no point in that kind of accusation. Polls are costly things to take and I cannot see why anyone would spend substantial sums of money on a poll and then falsify the results.
The Canadian institute of public opinion which is the Gallup poll in this country has some 500 people working continuously on a wide variety of subjects across the nation all the time. Their work embraces polls concerning the voting intentions of the electorate, not just at the time of an election but throughout the year every year. The hon. member says there is no guarantee that polls are taken on a regular sample basis. I do not know what he means by a guarantee but I do know that the Canadian institute of public opinion conducts a political poll every eight weeks. It describes its services as "a snapshot of voting intentions" taken not on election day or just before election day, but continuously thoughout the years. It is a political poll taken on a regular sample basis.

In conclusion may I say I condemn this bill not only as a manifestation of arrogant paternalism but also as a menace to fundamental freedoms. What right have we, the elected representatives of the people, to place any kind of restraint upon expressions of opinion? If the socialists would pay a little more attention to those expressions of opinion instead of trying to censor them they might learn something of what the people are thinking and be a little better off.
This bill is a veritable iron curtain behind which the socialists seek to hide their own inadequacies. It occurs to me the mere introduction of this bill is an indictment against the C.C.F. party and certainly a warning to the Canadian people. The socialists would impose their will upon the free expression of opinion of a free people. I hope, just as the hon. member for Timiskaming said, that we may have a vote on this amendment so that every responsible member of parliament may have the opportunity of standing up in this house and being counted on the side of freedom.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the bill which is before us for discussion this afternoon were to pass it would be in my opinion extremely difficult to enact it. What is to hinder the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) or any other hon. member appearing on a public platform or before a gathering of news people and predicting the result of a coming election by releasing the findings they have gathered from the reports sent in by their district organizers? Are we to make this a crime? Are we to make it unlawful to mention this from a platform? Any piece of legislation which having been put on the statute books is ignored or not enforced is to my mind serving only to clutter the administration of justice and to bring other worthwhile legislation into disrepute.
The newspaper people who travel across the country with the leaders of political parties during campaigns are entitled to and indeed are expected to express their opinions as to what people in the country are thinking and I do not believe we can bring in legislation to counter what the people of this country want and expect in the way of news.
A large number of people in this great country of ours are undecided as to how they should vote. Being human they naturally want to be on the winning side so that after an election they will be in a position to tell their friends that they were clever enough to have picked the winning candidate or the winning party. This is an unfortunate

situation because it indicates a lack of political education but, like the poor, this type is always with us.
I cannot see how any great harm could be caused by a straw vote which is only an indication of how the people are thinking at the particular time the poll is taken. Something could happen which would cause the voting population to veer completely around and vote in an entirely different fashion. Being so closely associated with our good neighbours to the south where the advance poll or Gallup poll has become almost a national institution I do not see how we in Canada could possibly prevent the publication of any advance prediction relating to a Canadian election.
The result of a poll among the general public concerning an election even when published does not mean that the outcome is guaranteed. Hon. members will recall during the election in which Mr. Harry Truman sought to become president of the United States all the newspapers and public polls were against him and yet by getting out and conducting an active election campaign he was able to win by a substantial majority. Apparently he was able to convince the people he was the better man. This illustrates the fact that although papers and magazines were full of how his opponent was taking the country by storm and that he might as well close up shop, nevertheless the polls were wrong and the man who had the backbone of public opinion behind him was he who won the election.
The hon. member who introduced this bill to amend the Canada Elections Act has said that he has no objection to the taking of public opinion polls in public schools and high schools by the pupils or in any other such places. Does he not realize that if the children who take these polls go home and report the results to their parents, in a number of cases they will have an effect on influencing the parents' votes. I know that during the last election in the constituency which I have the honour to represent my daughter was a school teacher and the children went back to their parents and practically told the parents that if they did not vote for my daughter's father they just would not have anything further to do with them, and that influenced quite a number in my favour. People want to be informed and I believe it is the duty of the newspapers to inform them. A poll does not constitute propaganda. The report of a public poll is only the announcement that in some measure a certain percentage of the population declares itself for or against a political party or a politician.
In my opinion these polls cannot prejudice our friends in any way because in this country
Canada Elections Act
people may often consider not so much the results of those polls but rather the party program and the candidates who are up for election. We saw that the results taken during the last election gave the facts, and the results were neither inaccurate nor dishonest, as the Canadian people sent to the house in the last election such a large Conservative majority.
I do not see any reason for the introduction of this bill, which seems to me to be only an excuse to use up the members' time when we could be gainfully employed in debating legislation that has merit to the country as a whole. I make these remarks as I am opposed to this bill and do not see any great merit in it. I believe this bill should not have been submitted to this house this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I think other hon. members on the government side have brought out most of the points that I think should be brought out in connection with this bill. In view of the lack of time I will not repeat their arguments but I would like to compliment them on their statements and on expressing my views so clearly. But as a former newspaperman who probably has had a great deal more experience in reporting and in editorial work, and knows more about the integrity of newspapers and their influence on the public than the proposer of Bill No. C-ll, I should like to bring out only two points which are involved in this proposed amendment.
In my opinion, they are two very vital points in our form of democracy which would

Canada Elections Act
be curtailed by this bill. These two points are freedom of the press and the right of each individual to all the information and expressions of opinion that he can possibly obtain, even during an election, or perhaps I should say particularly during an election. Any denial of those rights, I am sure, will not come from this government.
The sponsor of this amendment, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), wants to have public opinion polls, what he calls straw votes, abolished by federal statute. The purpose of this amendment, as was pointed out by the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken), is to prohibit and make punishable as an illegal practice the publication in any manner before election day of the results of a straw vote or polls of the political opinions of the electors. All I can say to this is that the hon. member for Timiskaming must have a very small regard for the mentality of Canadian voters. Perhaps he has reason for this poor opinion. I have a much higher regard for those who mark their ballots in federal elections. By inference, Mr. Speaker, the sponsor of this bill is saying that Canadian voters have no minds of their own, and, like a flock of sheep, will cast their ballots after having themselves directed in one direction by newspaper quotations and headlines and by publication of what the mover calls straw votes. I suggest that this is a very poor picture of our electorate. It is a picture that is not borne out by recent elections.
The Canadian voters have minds of their own and exercise their franchise as they see fit, and are not told how to vote by any newspaper headlines. I see nothing wrong with publication of straw votes in an election campaign. As I have said, straw votes are part of public opinion polls, and public opinion polls are part of public education. Public education has brought the Canadian people to the high level of living and, I might say, the high level of government that we now enjoy.
I should like to conclude with strong support for freedom of the press. The Canadian people want to be informed and it is the duty of our newspapers to inform them. As you know, Mr. Speaker, on most days when orders of the day are called the press gallery is filled with reporters and their job is to inform the Canadian people. Again, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that public opinion polls have the influence on voters that the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) fears they have. I think that during an election campaign Canadian voters consider the programs of the various parties as they are presented to them on the platform and they also consider the ability of the candidates. In my opinion,

therefore, members of this house should show their confidence in the clear thinking of the Canadian electorate by voting against the motion.

This list is a long one, comprising virtually all growers in Canada. My purpose in placing this list on the record is to show that requests coming from the council are in no wise sectional but rather the unanimous decision of a representative body. You will see that this can mean only one thing, and that is an ideal relationship between the council and the government, particularly with the Department of Agriculture. This has long been recognized by the department and I need only quote the words of a former minister of agriculture, Mr. Gardiner, to this effect, when he stated in Hansard of Friday, July 24, 1942, at page 4697 as follows:
I want to say . . . that the Department of Agriculture and I as minister greatly appreciate the associations that have existed between the horticultural council and the department . . . Since I have had the privilege of being Minister of Agriculture the one group of farm producers who have maintained ideal relationships between the department and their industry are those people who are associated with the horticultural council . . . They have not asked the department or the government to be represented in certain places. They set up an organization of their own; they have made known their needs and seen to it that the department at all times knew what their organization thought ought to be done. They have worked consistently at the task of taking care of the interests of their producers. They have not wasted any of their energies in other directions. While the thanks of the growers of fruit, and particularly the apple growers, have been extended to the department officials and to myself as minister, I must say that a great part of the credit is due to the fact that the industry has been so well organized under the council ... I think they found the officials of the different departments ready to sit down with

them to work out their problems. The problem could not be dealt with entirely by the Department of Agriculture. The Department of Finance plays a considerable part . . . and also the Department of Trade and Commerce when the problem is associated with trade outside of Canada. That organization at all times has been well informed not only with regard to their own industry here, but also with regard to the possibilities of marketing their products. They have stayed with the job until they, in co-operation with our officials, have worked out plans which would be helpful.
May I also quote Mr. Stirling, a former Conservative member of this house, who for many years ably represented his constituency. His remarks followed those made by Mr. Gardiner and are reported in the same edition of Hansard:
I should like to present my own thanks to the minister tor the way in which he has referred to the Canadian Horticultural Council. I feel sure that the recognition which he has given this evening will be greatly appreciated by the many associations which go to make up that council.
So long as I have been a member of this house, in my endeavours to represent the fruit and vegetable growers of the part of Canada that I represent, it has been of very great assistance to me to be able to turn to the information always available through the secretary of the horticultural council.
May I add my own appreciation of the services provided by the council? I may say in passing that they were kind enough to have me at their last three-day meeting in Ottawa. I have dealt with this council at length, because I wish hon. members to know more about it. This body-the Canadian Horticultural Council-is a sincere one. There is nothing sectional in its ambitions. The government knows, through its long association with the council, that the requests made by it have been thoroughly studied and debated, and it is for this reason that the government respects the council's decision.
You will understand now, Mr. Speaker, that I have no hesitation about raising my final point, which is this: that the government should give effect to the fair value for duty section which applies to fruits and vegetables. You will recall that it was passed last year under the amendment to the Customs Act, namely paragraph (b) subsection 7 of section 40A. However-and this should be underlined -this was only to take effect upon proclamation, and to date the section has yet to be proclaimed. The Canadian Horticultural Council has always recognized the principle of fair value for duty. They feel that it is an absolutely necessary safeguard against distress selling or, as we say otherwise, the importation of fruit and vegetables into this country at fire sale prices. I say that the council has always recognized the principle of fair value for duty, but perhaps it would be better to say that they have fought for it since the inception of the council in 1922.
The Budget-Mr. Pearson
Finally, I subscribe to this principle because I have seen the effects of distress selling in my own constituency, and I am sure many hon. members here have themselves seen the effect of distress selling in their own ridings. I myself have seen the gradual deterioration of a well established industry. It is a hard thing to consider that at best our growers can only realize a second rate price for the goods they produce. Fair value for duty is, I think it is fair to say, the answer to this problem, and I now ask the government to give early and earnest consideration to this establishment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that my hon. friend who has preceded me will forgive me if I do not follow him into the fruit orchards and vegetables gardens of the lovely part of the world from which he comes. I propose to deal with some more general aspects of the budget, of the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in introducing it and, indeed, of the speech which he made this afternoon in defending it.
I regret that the Minister of Finance is not in his place but I quite realize that he is filling an important public engagement at which I know those who sit on the opposite side of the table will have a greater opportunity of asking him questions with regard to some of his spectacular statements than we had in the house this afternoon. However, the absence of the minister does not deter me from complimenting him on his energy and his industry and on what I might call the massive performance of his budget speech which, according to some commentators and onlookers, may be his last. If this should be the case I think we can say quite sincerely that he has been the greatest minister of finance that Canada has had since Mr. Walter Harris.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That, of course, is not a new joke. That has been used several times.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In saying this I do not overlook the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) was acting minister of finance, I think, though for a very short time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No; that last statement was no more accurate than the other one.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can congratulate the Minister of Finance on that score at least, and I do it very sincerely, for I have a real admiration for him though at times I find it difficult to understand how a man who can be so amiable in private conversation can, when he debates in the house or on the hustings, indulge in what I can only call such voluble irascibility. I cannot, however,

The Budget-Mr. Pearson compliment the minister on either the form or the content of his budget speech which I thought-and nothing he has said this afternoon has removed that thought-was less than candid and more than normally partisan in many places.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) in a report which he apparently makes periodically from parliament hill to the Kentville Advertiser described this budget very accurately indeed in the latest of these reports which I have seen as "bitter and disagreeable medicine". Well, that seems to be the verdict in the country. A paper which circulates widely in my own constituency-a very good newspaper, though a very Conservative paper-The Sault Star- called it a vexing disappointment. The Globe and Mail called it worse than that.
The budget does indeed show a startling contrast between past promises and present performance and nothing that the Minister of Finance said this afternoon has altered our view on this score. To hon. members on the government side that contrast must have been disheartening. To the country it is disillusioning.
There was an interesting contrast, too, between the approach of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue to the budget in so far as the question of promises is concerned. The burden of the remarks of the Minister of Finance this afternoon on this aspect of the subject was, as it were, "We did not make the promises but we are keeping them." One part of the remarks made by the Minister of National Revenue the other night was to the effect that they made them but they are of two kinds. He went on to say as reported at page 2624 of Hansard of April 13, 1959:
-there is no doubt that promises of any kind, whether pre-election promises or otherwise, should be honoured and respected so far as circumstances will possibly permit-
Indeed, the Minister of National Revenue has now divided political promises into two kinds, those made outside the house and those made inside the house, first and second class promises. Surely there is sufficient justification in those words and their reflection in government policy for the charge which is implicit in our amendment on which we will be voting this evening, the charge that this administration has elevated expediency into a principle and practice of government. Surely that is the main reason why this government has lost standing in the country so soon after its electoral triumph of a year ago.
Perhaps, however, hon. gentlemen opposite are beginning to learn. I confess that this


budget shows some signs of it. They are perhaps beginning to learn that every promise conceived by an advertising director who now directs a political party and tossed emotionally and irresponsibly to the electorate-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the tax cuts?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will come to that. Perhaps they are beginning to learn that such actions have fiscal and economic consequences.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will come to grief if you continue.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At this time the Prime Minister has indeed called the political tune but it is the people who are paying the piper. That is perhaps why one prominent Canadian business man has called this budget the chicken roosting budget, and no crowing by the Minister of Finance or his faithful backbench followers can conceal that fact. Perhaps an even better designation for this budget would be the budget of the morning after two nights before.
Events are now catching up with the minister and his colleagues. Their pilgrims' progress from the fantasies of the hustings to the realities of the treasury benches has been slow, painful and very expensive for the country. If, however, this progress should result in planned and well thought out economic and fiscal policies in the future based on sound economic principles and not on the whims and emotions of party pressures and party advantage, something at least will have been salvaged from the partisan promissory activity of two elections.
The Minister of Finance this afternoon was guilty of a course of action of which he and some of his colleagues have been guilty before. When they are in trouble and when it is difficult for them to explain the problems that face them in the economic and financial fields-and the minister was having some difficulty in that regard this afternoon, especially when he got into the field of monetary policy-they blame it all on world conditions. They say the United States or some other international factor is to blame.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the Minister of Finance, without the kind of smile which he has on his face now, attacked our estimates of the deficit for last year and my own in particular -because I did undoubtedly make an estimate and so did the Canada tax foundation of almost $1 billion-we said the deficit would be $835 million based on the minister's own calculations of revenue. Taking into account the national defence expenditure fund that would have been $950 million as my hon. friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) pointed out yesterday. On the basis of the revenue forecast by the minister himself, the estimates we made earlier and which the minister said had done so much damage to the country-estimates of almost $1 billion, on those estimates based on the minister's own calculations of revenue and not ours- he had to change them later, the deficit would have been $950 million.
As it is, his revenue has exceeded his estimates. He had a few windfalls, one due in no small part to the increased interest rate which gave the Bank of Canada a slightly larger profit than they had calculated, I think $22 million larger. But whatever the
The Budget-Mr. Pearson figure may be, last year's deficit was the highest peacetime deficit in our history, a record.
The estimated budgetary deficit this year is not $393 million but $435 million, if we include, as we should, the current deficit on the old age security fund. That makes a two-year budgetary deficit of $1,270 million, which is a record however you look at it. It makes the budgetary and non-budgetary deficit for 1958-59, $1,200 million, well over the $1 billion which the minister tosses back to us. His estimated cash deficit, budgetary and non-budgetary, for the current year 1959-60 is $850 million. Therefore, we have a cash deficit for two years of over $2 billion, which is another record broken. We had a deficit last year in the old age pension fund of $184 million and a year's drop in the unemployment insurance fund of $242 million, two more records. We have an increase in one year in the national debt of $1,400 million, which is a peacetime record in our history and which almost wipes out the reductions made in 10 years to the national debt because of prudent and wise Liberal financial administration.
I will give a few more records. From December 31, 1957 to December 31, 1958 we had an increase in the money supply of $1,324 million, or more than 11 per cent, which is greater than the total cash deficit for that year, and that is a record. We also have an increase in taxes in one year-not the figure the Prime Minister used on television last night-of $352 million, and we have that while, according to the figures which were released today for March, more than half a million men are still out of work. That is another record; that is another first, Mr. Speaker. We have an increase in the number of government employees, also a new record.
Then we come to expenditures for 1958, 1959 and 1960, something about which the Minister of Finance had a good deal to say this afternoon in showing how hard the treasury board-he is the chairman of the treasury board-had worked to keep expenses down. Last year, as the house knows, the expenditures were $5,387 million, the highest in any year, peace or war, in our history, and $538 million above the figure for the last year of Liberal administration.
We on this side of the house remember how the hon. members on the other side, when they were over here and when they were on the hustings, were going to save $500 million out of government expenditures because of waste and extravagance. What have they done? They have added $538 million to government expenditures. That was another record until it was exceeded by

The Budget-Mr. Pearson the budgetary estimates tor 1959-60, which reached $5,660 million. These expenditures for 1959-60, which the minister gave the other night in the house, are $165 million more than the amount submitted in the main estimates previously. But it is not likely that that will be enough to deal with the extra expenditures of government, because out of this $165 million the minister has to find amounts under the Agricultural Stabilization Act; he has to find $51 million for the C.N.R. deficit; he has to find assistance, if any to western grain producers; he has to find increases, if any, in the salaries of civil servants; and he has to find enough for the usual and further supplementaries. But with all these increases in government expenditures, the capital expenditures, as I shall try to show in a	momentthese are the employment expenditures, Mr. Speaker, at a time when we need employment -are not higher this year, they are lower. Therefore, the level of expenditures generally will not likely make any material contribution to a lower level of unemployment but they are likely to make a contribution to a higher level of inflationary pressures.
I have a table here comparing the main estimates-and this is not the kind of comparison which is fair, not in comparing the main estimates of one year with the main and supplementary estimates of another, as the minister has done more than once in the house-of 1958-59 with the main estimates of 1959-60. I have taken the figures for one of those years from the summary of standard objects of expenditure and special categories which is attached to the estimate book which we received some time ago. If you look at the expenditures in this way you get a very interesting idea of where the increases and decreases are. Civil salaries and wages are up in the current year by $24 million, and the government was going to cut down civil service expenditures. Here is an interesting item. Perhaps this has a bearing on what the hon. member for Essex East said last night in his peroration. He expressed the hope that the minister might move up or, if it suited him, he might move down or, at least, he said the minister should move. The minister and his colleagues are moving all right, because under the item "travelling and removal expenses" we have an increase of $9 million in the current estimates over last year. I know this government had done a good deal of travelling, Mr. Speaker, but I did not know that it added up to a $9 million increase in our expenditures.
We remember also how the minister and his friends, when they were on this side of the house, inveighed against the government of the day for wastage on telephones, telegrams,

publication of departmental reports and all that kind of thing. Well, telephones and telegrams and all that sort of thing are up over $2 million in 1959-60 and the publication of departmental reports should be down because we have the greatest difficulty in getting departmental reports circulated. We assumed that naturally the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) especially was saving money. Well, the publication of departmental reports-

speechtext: When are you going to steal another one?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-this year is up $1 million. On exhibits and advertising-I do not know how much of this goes to the McKim advertising company-we have a figure of $11,800,000 this year; but, Mr. Speaker, when we get to the summary of standard objects that deal with capital expenditures, the things that make jobs-and we have 525,000 people looking for jobs in this country-when we get to buildings and works, construction or acquisition, repairs and upkeep, we have a decrease of $68 million. So much for the great billion dollar works program which we heard so much about. These record increases, Mr. Speaker, come from a government elected on a solemn undertaking to reduce the cost of government and eliminate all waste and extravagance so as to increase services without raising taxes. At one stage indeed they were going to appoint a royal commission to look into the civil service and cut out all these unnecessary costs.
When the minister told us this afternoon that we have been misquoting and misrepresenting promises which were never made, may I say there is one promise dealing with this which has already been put on the record of Hansard. I would not put it on again tonight if it were not for the minister's vehement denial this afternoon that it was ever made. I refer to the promise made on Empire Day, May 24, 1957, over the C.B.C. to the people of Canada by the Prime Minister, and I will repeat once again these immortal words. He said:
The Liberals tell you it is not possible to lower taxes and raise pensions at the same time. Give us a chance-
And he got the chance.
-we'll show you.
But the Minister of Finance says that no such promise was ever made. Lest the minister of National Revenue might dismiss this kind of statement as the bubbling over of an election campaign, let me add some other words also spoken by the Prime Minister. I quote from another statement he made:
My idea of politics is that promises should only be made that can be effectuated.

In other words, promises that are made should be kept, which is a simpler Anglo-Saxon word than "effectuated". Well, let us look at some more records. There is another first in our financial history. We have had recently rising prices in a period of persistent recession or pause or whatever you want to call it. The average treasury bill rate for last week, and the Minister of Finance did not tell us about this this afternoon, was 4.61 per cent, an all-time high in this country, compared with a treasury bill rate on July 30, 1958 of .87, or an increase of 530 per cent during that period of time. The minister is inclined to blame this on the United States so perhaps he will listen to this. The present rate in Canada is 60 per cent higher than that in the United States where the treasury bill rate is 3 per cent, so let us not blame that development in this country on the Americans. So much for the Tory condemnation of dear money.
Where are the other vows of yesterday? Where is the 15 per cent trade diversion? That figured largely in a lot of talk not so very long ago but I can understand why members of the government are very silent about it now in the light of what has happened. In 1958 the United Kingdom's unfavourable balance with Canada widened, and the United Kingdom is the country that was going to be helped by this diversion. It rose from $221 million to $254 million. That is diversion the wrong way. In the first three months of 1959 imports from the United States into this country, which were to be diverted, are up 4 per cent and imports from the United Kingdom, which was to benefit by the diversion, are down 8 per cent compared with the same period in 1958. These are figures from the bureau of statistics survey and not from the Fleming or Martin statistical services.
No wonder, that the president of the board of trade, Sir David Eccles, complained in a speech in London on February 5 to the Canadian chamber of commerce, I believe, that Canada had done little to improve her purchases from Britain. He is reported as saying in what was referred to in the press as a rebuke to Canada:
No other country sold to us so much more than it bought.
Then, Mr. Speaker, where is the cure for unemployment through that billion dollar public works project which has also disappeared? Where is the new deal for the provinces and the municipalities? Where is parity, not charity, for the farmers? Where is that stand-up policy to the United States that was to prevent restrictions on our exports and unfair competition in surplus disposal programs? Where is this policy that was going
The Budget-Mr. Pearson to protect our sovereignty against United States economic and financial control?
On March 9, the Prime Minister on the program "The Nation's Business" had this among other interesting things to say, and I quote from the text of his broadcast as issued from his office:
It was because I knew Canadians felt so strongly about the necessity of preserving Canada's destiny that I have advocated and the government has launched its national development policy to push back our northern frontiers. The result of our action has been that in the last several weeks over 75 million acres in northern Canada have been taken up for oil and mineral development, and I want to underline this-
The Prime Minister is doing the underlining, not I.
-that this is a major means to preserve our sovereignty.
Then he went on to say, "Let us be realistic." Well, Mr. Speaker, I will try to be realistic and indicate the facts as we secured them from the minister concerned. Of all these millions of acres taken up for oil and mineral development to protect and preserve the sovereignty of Canada, 95 per cent of the leases went to United States firms or Canadian subsidiaries of United States firms. This is the way we are protecting our Canadian sovereignty.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank you again, Mr. Speaker. In former days, and by that I mean days before the present Minister of Finance, the prospects for the coming year were usually given in considerable detail in the budget speech. But the present Minister of Finance has practically eliminated this customary and important section from his budget speech for this year, massive a performance though it was. In 1958 five pages of Hansard were devoted to the prospects for the forthcoming year. This budget speech had one paragraph to forecast economic conditions in 1959-60. It had one paragraph on the forecast of the gross national product which is the basis for estimating a revenue and thereby establishing a deficit or a surplus. All the minister had to say this year, was that, assuming normal crops, stable prices and no untoward external events, there should be a gross national product of about $34.5 billion, or a 7 per cent increase. He made no attempt then to justify this optimistic forecast, and he made no attempt to justify it this afternoon. It is a forecast which has been dismissed by many experts, and I will name mine, although he did not name his this afternoon. They include the Canadian tax foundation, the financial editor of the Montreal Gazette, and indeed the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, which in its submission to the government forecast a gross physical output in 1959-60 of approximately 1 per cent, not 7 per cent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us look at the figures. For the first quarter of 1959 the estimate is a 4 per cent increase. To achieve 7 per cent for the whole year, Mr. Speaker, that 4 per cent would have to increase to 6 per cent in the second quarter, 8 per cent in the third quarter and 10 per cent in the last quarter, without any increase in prices. Let us hope the minister's calculations in this regard are not as far out as they were last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or yours.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

My calculations on this point last year, as stated in my budget speech, were that the minister was too optimistic. The minister estimated a gross national product increase of 2 per cent, and with stable prices what did he get? He got 0.6 per cent, I think. How much further out could you be than that? The minister always forgets the qualification of stable prices when he is arguing about that. Let us hope for the good of the country that he is not as inaccurate this year as he was last year. He does not give us any basis for his optimism. He does not say it is due to an increased level of investment, because if he did say that he would be contradicted by his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill)-although that is no new experience for ministers of this government- who in his departmental report on private and public investment in Canada for 1959 said that the level of investment would likely be down 1.2 per cent in 1959-60. He could not surely have based his optimistic calculation on exports, because although the government has made a great deal of the export situation during the year which has just passed, the figures for the first three months of 1959 show a decrease of 3 per cent, whereas imports are up 5 per cent.
There are some very dangerous features in our export situation. In particular, one of the most important export products we have in this country is uranium. What have we learned about that recently? The other day in the house the minister said that for the first time in a year he had been able to go down to Washington to see the head of the atomic energy commission of the United States in regard to a product the importance of which is indicated by the fact that during this current year, if all goes well, we will be exporting to the United States about $325 million worth. That $325 million, or whatever the amount may be, depends on a contract made by the previous Canadian government with the United States.
That contract comes up for renewal in 1961, and in April, 1959 the minister at last goes down to Washington to discuss this matter with his opposite number in the United States government. He spent a whole day in Washington. I hope he had a profitable time, but I have some doubt about the profitability of his visit when I realize that within five days of his return a senior official of the atomic energy commission makes a public statement in Colorado, the centre of the United States uranium production industry, to the effect that after 1962, 80 per cent of the United States requirements for uranium will be met from United States sources.

To say the least, that is a discourteous way to treat a Canadian minister to make such a statement, only a few days after he had been down to Washington, I hope to impress upon the United States government, not only the importance of this export trade but also the fact that the United States government has a moral duty to take up those contracts. Because it was not many years ago when they got down on their knees and begged the Canadian government to spend all its energy and resources in order to develop this product for United States consumption. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thus our export trade will be in some difficulties which I hope the government will be able to surmount. I wonder if it is consumer expenditure on which the government intends to rely for its 7 per cent increase? It might be well to remember that the rise in consumer incomes will be partly offset by increased taxation and higher prices and that it cannot in any event be sufficient to provide a 7 per cent increase in real terms of gross national product. The minister also touched on the changing role of inventories. I suggest that his prediction of a 7 per cent increase may well be too optimistic, and that if the hon. gentleman is wrong in this calculation the effect on employment opportunities in 1959 and 1960 in this country will be very bad indeed.
Let us look at the effect on employment. When in the budget debate a year ago, we did our duty by calling attention to some of
2914	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Pearson the discouraging possibilities in the employment picture we were sneered at, as we were this afternoon, by the Minister of Finance as being prophets of doom and gloom. A year ago we told the government that the unemployment level throughout 1958 would remain high, and we were laughed at. This government optimism of that time is proving to be false, and our forecasts, which were dismissed then as expressions of doom and gloom, have shown themselves to have been correct.
The action taken by the government last year to meet the employment difficulties was both too late and too little, as the establishment of the winter work program showed. Employment in this country varies closely, though of course with an inevitable lag, in accordance with the physical volume of our gross national product. In 1958, on an average, 6.6 per cent of our labour force was unemployed during the year. The estimated increase in our labour force for 1959 is 2.5 per cent. Therefore, if our gross national product remains constant, 9 per cent of our people will likely to be out of work in the current year. If only a 4 to 5 per cent increase in the volume of the gross national product is achieved-and that is the estimate of the tax foundation-that would mean that during the current year we would have, on the average, more than 300,000 people unemployed in this country which would be the second highest level in the post war period. Thus, notwithstanding the hon. gentleman's facile optimism on this score, the problem of unemployment remains and is likely to remain throughout the year.
Along with this there is a second serious problem-though one would never know it from the minister's budget statement-and that is the problem of increasing prices along with persistant unemployment. Though inflation remains a problem parallel with that presented by unemployment, the minister, in a somewhat brief reference in his budget speech to inflation, said merely that he was against it, but that he did not see any evidence of overt inflation in the coming year. The danger, he said, was only that of potential inflationary pressures. Believe me, in the light of the fiscal and monetary situation of this country and the amount of money that the minister, according to his own calculations, has to raise this year, that danger of potential inflationary pressures is a very real one indeed.
The minister tried to make us feel a little happier about this by pointing out-and he was quite right-that the consumer price index had declined slightly since November. I think that is the case. But he did not point out that since November the wholesale price


index has been rising

1.7 per cent-and the wholesale price index has a better coverage and is a better reflection of the movement of prices and costs than the retail price index though it usually precedes the retail index in its changes. The minister has once again in this budget rejected the doctrine of the inevitability of creeping inflation and yet-and I know I will be told that I am a prophet of doom and gloom when I say this-even if we have a boom in 1959-and we are not going to have a boom in 1959-I believe that prices will rise in the current year. There is a great deal of evidence, unfortunately, to support that view.
The increased taxation imposed by this budget will mean-indeed, it has already meant-an opportunity for further increases in the prices of goods and services to producers; and any further increase in the money supply-and there is a real danger of that- will certainly expedite that process. Last year we had a tremendous increase in the money supply. I think it amounted to $1,400 million. The full inflationary effect of that increase was not realized because the recession had reduced what the economists call the velocity of its circulation. This year, however, any progress toward recovery-and we are making progress toward recovery- will serve to remove any such brake, and inflationary pressures will consequently be greater.
To sum up, last year we had mounting unemployment and some inflation in the midst of recession. This year there should be less, but still serious, unemployment and a greater danger of inflation. The paradox of this dual problem, this double dilemma, will persist and will remain a challenge to a government which has not yet shown that it has any effective plan to meet this challenge.
When we on this side talk in this way someone on the other side usually interjects to ask: what would you have done or what else could the government have done? I would remind the hon. gentleman that I went into this matter in considerable detail in the speech I made during the debate on the address, a speech which the minister conveniently forgot this afternoon when he twitted me for not having found alternative policies.
But I say to the minister and his colleagues that they could, a year and a half ago, have introduced into this house a budget making provision for a planned program of expenditure designed to extend possibilities of employment and which could later have been quickly and easily readjusted so as to meet conditions asJ they changed^ The ordinary expenditures of government could have been

kept down-but they were not kept down- and increases in the expenditure of government-and there would have had to be some increases, of course, one and a half years ago-could have been directed to areas where unemployment was greatest and to capital projects which would have had the maximum effect in terms of jobs.
One and a half years ago the government could have realized, as we on this side realized, that unemployment would be high all through 1958. They could have worked out a winter works program in the spring of last year, not in the fall of 1958, just as they should be working out such a program now for the current year.
What did they do? They charged along piling up promises and commitments, and increasing departmental commitments and expenditures, without developing, as the Toronto Globe and Mail pointed out to them, any overall fiscal policy whatever. All that the Minister of Finance could say to us in reply to that charge was: "What kind of policy would you adopt?"
Last year the fiscal proposals of this government were based on electoral necessity. This year they are based on inescapable financial necessity. As a result we have the worst of three worlds abnormal unemployment, rising prices and higher taxes. The minister, of course, has made a virtue of the fact that people seem resigned to the new Conservative policy. If that resignation exists I assure the minister, if he needs any assurance, that it will turn to bitter anger if in spite of these higher taxes both serious unemployment and higher prices persist throughout the current year.
The amount of the minister's new taxes is $352 million and this will have a serious impact. He has taken some credit for the fact that it is spread over the community in a way in which those who are most able to pay do pay. But of the $352 million the sum of $84 million will come from corporation income taxes which now in most cases can be transferred to the ultimate consumer and which is becoming more and more assimilated in our economy to a sales tax. The sum of $75 million of the $352 million comes from an additional old age security tax, 1 per cent of personal incomes. That will certainly fall most heavily on the lower income groups. Of the $352 million the sum of $93 million is sales tax, and how the minister when he was on this side of the house used to criticize sales taxes.

That is what he said. That is the position he took. That is why we have the right to be suspicious of the bona tides of this government when it introduces a budget of this kind. How can we dissociate the former views of these men from the views they hold at this time without accusing them of hyprocrisy or inconsistency?
Let me remind hon. gentlemen opposite of what the Minister of Finance said in 1950, and repeated every year since then. I refer to a statement of the minister reported at page 713 of Hansard of September 13, 1950:
I wish to put myself on record-
And I will put the minister on record again.
I wish to put myself on record, as I have on similar occasions in the past, with regard to taxes of this nature-
That is sales taxes.
-by saying that they are not the kind of taxes that ought to be encouraged by the House of Commons. They are discriminatory against people of small means.
Are they?

Are they?
-and in the third place the consumer pays for more than the tax. The consumer pays the original tax plus the wholesalers' mark-up on the tax, plus the retailer's mark-up on the mark-up on the tax. In that way you will find that in most cases what the consumer pays, by reason of the imposition of the tax, is just about twice as much as the government receives by way of tax levied at the manufacturer's level.
Those words were spoken by the Minister of Finance in 1950. If the minister still feels that way about sales tax why did he bring in the kind of budget he did? The minister is a very determined person and does not change his mind easily. Why did he not do away with increased sales taxes? What could have convinced him to change his mind?

Certainly not the Liberal party.

The minister told us in his budget speech and again this afternoon that decision of his government about expenditures, about the deficit and about taxes result from the systematic application of a sound and considered fiscal policy. I say that the evidence shows that that is nonsense, and that these decisions embodied in this budget result from fiscal necessities, brought about by electoral irresponsibilities.
The minister attempted to rationalize all of this in his budget speech. I quite admit he did try to make a kind of academic argument for the change which apparently someone brought about in his way of economic thinking. He tried to rationalize his thinking in a very odd intellectual exercise, considering his past views and past assertions. The minister has now become a follower of the man who used to be laughed at so often in this house by the minister and those who sit on that side of the house. I remember that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell) as he then was, who is now Minister without Portfolio, used to laugh along with my friend the Minister of Finance. In any event, Mr. Speaker, in 1959, a new disciple of Keynes is born, a convert who was once one of the most violent of unbelievers. But how can we possibly have faith in the minister until he publicly recants his former views? The Minister of Finance is now on record as being in favour of anti-cyclical budgets. He has caught what he used to call a disease. Paul Samuelson described the impact of "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money", published by Keynes in 1936, as follows:
The general theory caught most economists under the age of 35 with the unexpected virulence of a disease first attacking and decimating an isolated tribe of south sea islanders. The government, however, and this is my concluding section of my remarks on the budget, Mr. Speaker, still makes excuses for all its trouble by the fable of its evil inheritance, that hoary old canard which really should be dropped by them. The minister says that the recession began in the spring of 1957 and we concealed it from the people. The Prime Minister repeats the fable at every possible opportunity, that a recession which in the fall of 1957 they claimed after four months in office did not exist began in the spring of 1957 and was concealed from the country and from them.
Mr. Speaker, let us dispose of this transparent fallacy once and for all by quoting from the government's own considered and expert analysis of the situation in the report "Economic Prospects for 1958" which the Minister of Trade and Commerce did his best to conceal from the house and from the country. If you want a good reason for that feeling about it let me quote this paragraph which disposes of this argument, surely, once and for all. This is from the minister's own report:
Overall physical activity reached a peak during late 1956 and early 1957 and the changes to the third quarter were quite minor, but have since become somewhat more pronounced. Total employment, on the other hand, continued to increase somewhat longer with employment in manufacturing reaching a peak by the middle of 1957 and total non-agricultural employment declining only in the fourth quarter of last year.
There it is, Mr. Speaker. Now let us deal with the position as we see it at this time. The economic position in this country is better than it was; otherwise we would be in a desperate situation indeed. I agree with the minister, and I have never denied it though he accuses us tonight of denying it,
The Budget-Mr. Pearson that there are some bright features in the economy which do presage recovery. The minister gave all the details. The Budget-Mr. Pearson
One of the editors of the Financial Post, John Macdonald, had this to say on March 28, and this is a very good description of what has happened to the government and to the country through the policy of the government. This man said:
The government is in the position of being obliged to throw water upon the inflationary fires of its own making.
Surely, no member of the government, no member on the other side, will deny that if action had been taken a year and a half ago, in the summer of 1958; if a budget had been introduced in the fall of that year; if there had been an accounting to the people of Canada; if there had been a statement of the economic difficulties, economic possibilities, economic dangers in this country; if action had been taken at that time to meet some of those problems we would not have been in the situation we have been in in the last year. It cannot be denied by any honest member of the government that at that time the government was more concerned with the forthcoming general election than with the economic and financial position of the country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, some of the fires that the government are trying to put out now-and we will give them full credit for the efforts they are making-are, as the Financial Post man said, of their own making.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I might complete my remarks by reading a paragraph from a Canadian paper because the Minister of Finance reproached me a few moments ago for taking my quotations from outside Canada. Here is a paragraph from the Peterborough Examiner. I apologize to the Minister of Finance for ending on what may be an unduly personal note. He knows that I do this in no unfriendly way.
The hon. member for Eglinton, the Minister of Finance, is a man who deserves our respect and admiration; he is as supple in his opinions and in his economics as a pitchman selling kickapoo- joy-juice,
I do not know what that is, Mr. Speaker, and I hope it is not alcoholic. Then the editorial goes on:
In flexibility he stands head and shoulders above his cabinet colleagues and for plugging a hole he is swiftly off the mark. It is being said in Toronto that his budget is aimed at the self-indulgent and rich; actually it calls all sections of the country to relieve the treasury from its financial plight.
That financial plight, is in large part at least the result of both bad management and bad faith on the part of the government. That is why we on this side have moved this amendment on which we will now proceed to vote and which we on this side will certainly strongly, sincerely and enthusiastically support.

subtopic: MARTIN F. RUSSELL
MARTIN F. RUSSELL
speechtext:
1.	Was Martin F. Russell, of Shippegan Gully, Gloucester county, New Brunswick, recently dismissed as temporary guardian for the range lights at Shippegan Gully?
2.	If so, on what date did this dismissal take place and for what reasons?
3.	What is the name and address of the guardian presently in charge of the said range lights?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of
Transport):
1 and 2. Following advice from the Caraquet chamber of commerce of a shift in the channel, it was necessary to make changes to the Shippegan Gully entrance range. A new structure for the front light was installed and the back light was relocated. At the same time, opportunity was taken to change both lights from oil to automatic battery operation. A Mr. Martin F. Roussel had been part time lightkeeper for these lights but with the change to automatic operation a lightkeeper was no longer necessary and his services as part time lightkeeper were
Questions
for this reason terminated effective October 1, 1958. A caretaker was considered to be adequate for the protection of the lights, and Mr. Roussel acted in that capacity on an entirely temporary basis from October 1, 1958, to January 15, 1959.
3.	As the shipping season has been closed, a permanent caretaker has not been selected up to now.

subtopic: TRANSPORTATION ALLOWANCES, RENOUS NAVAL DEPOT
TRANSPORTATION ALLOWANCES, RENOUS NAVAL DEPOT
speechtext:
1.	Is it proposed to make changes in transportation allowances for civilian personnel engaged at the Renous Naval Ammunition Depot, Renous, New Brunswick?
2.	If so, what changes will be made and when will they be effective?
Answer by: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
1 and 2. The transportation allowance regulations for civilian personnel employed at the naval ammunition depot at Renous, N.B. are under review. Until this review is completed the present regulations will remain in effect.
